name: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
subtitle: A gentle first look at how AI learns, for school pupils aged nine and above, with almost no code to begin with.

curriculum.title: What Artificial Intelligence Really Is
topics: Sorting everyday gadgets into those that learn from data and those that simply follow fixed rules
Describing in your own words what makes a task easy for people but surprisingly hard for computers
Playing a guessing game to see how a machine narrows down choices by asking one good question at a time
Meeting the idea of an algorithm through familiar recipes, bus directions and morning routines
Spotting AI already at work in voice assistants, photo tagging and video recommendations
Discussing what computers are still very poor at, from humour to ordinary common sense
Drawing a simple diagram showing data going in, a model in the middle and a prediction coming out

curriculum.title: How Machines Learn from Examples
topics: Collecting a small set of examples together and labelling each one carefully by hand
Watching how adding more examples and better labels changes what the model ends up learning
Learning the difference between learning from labelled answers and sorting things into groups with no labels at all
Playing a paper-and-pencil game in which you act as the model and update your own guesses after every mistake
Understanding features as the clues a model looks at, such as colour, size or shape
Seeing what goes wrong when every single training example comes from one narrow source
Explaining why a model can be confidently wrong and why that matters so much for the people using it

curriculum.title: Training Your First Models Without Writing Code
topics: Training an image classifier with a webcam by showing it dozens of examples of each class
Testing your trained model on pictures it has never seen and noting exactly where it stumbles
Improving accuracy by adding more varied examples rather than simply more of the same ones
Training a sound model that can tell a clap apart from a whistle even in a noisy room
Connecting a trained model to a block-based program so an on-screen character reacts to what the camera sees
Building a small rule-based chatbot and noticing precisely where its scripted replies break down
Keeping a simple experiment diary of what you changed and what happened to the results

curriculum.title: Teaching a Computer with Simple Code
topics: Writing your first few lines of Python to print a message, calculate a sum and store an answer
Making a list of numbers and asking the computer for the largest, smallest and average value
Plotting a handful of data points on a chart and describing the pattern you can see
Drawing a straight line through scattered points and using it to predict a brand new value
Training a ready-made classifier on a small tidy dataset of flowers or fruits and reading the score it earns
Changing one setting at a time and observing carefully whether that score rises or falls
Explaining your small programme line by line to a parent, teacher or classmate

curriculum.title: AI in the Real World and Your Showcase Project
topics: Looking at how AI is helping doctors, farmers and shopkeepers across India right now
Debating whether it is fair for a computer to decide who receives a loan or a school place
Discovering how bias creeps in when the training data does not represent everybody equally
Agreeing a simple set of ground rules for using AI honestly in your own schoolwork
Planning a showcase project that solves one small problem in your home or classroom
Gathering your own examples, training the model and testing it on real users for feedback
Presenting the finished project with a poster and a short live demonstration
Reflecting honestly on what you would improve given another month to work on it

name: Python Programming for Beginners
subtitle: Gentle live Python classes for first-time young coders, built around turtle drawings and small games.

curriculum.title: Level 1 · Meeting Python
topics: Opening a Python editor with your tutor and running one line of code that prints a message on the screen.
Making the computer print your name, your school and your favourite colour, one line under another.
Keeping a number or a word in a variable, then changing it later and printing it again.
Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing to work out a pocket-money total in rupees.
Asking a question with input and using the answer the person typed on the very next line.
Saving your work in a file with a sensible name so that you can open it again next class.
Reading a friendly error message, spotting the spelling mistake it points at and fixing it yourself.

curriculum.title: Level 2 · Drawing with the Turtle
topics: Bringing the turtle onto the screen and moving it forward, backward, left and right.
Drawing squares, triangles and stars by repeating the same few instructions.
Working out the turn for any regular shape by dividing a full 360-degree turn by the number of sides.
Changing the pen colour, the pen thickness and the background so that a drawing looks attractive.
Lifting and putting down the pen so the turtle can move without leaving a line behind it.
Filling shapes with colour to draw a house, a kite or a simple rangoli pattern.
Combining several shapes into one picture and saving it so you can show it at home.

curriculum.title: Level 3 · Making Choices and Repeating Steps
topics: Comparing two numbers with the greater-than, less-than and equal-to signs and printing what you find.
Using if and else so the computer replies one way to a right answer and another way to a wrong one.
Adding elif to handle three or more possibilities, such as the grade bands for test marks.
Repeating instructions a fixed number of times with a for loop and a counter you can watch.
Repeating until something changes with a while loop, such as guessing a hidden number.
Putting a choice inside a loop to build a short quiz that keeps the score as it goes.
Tracing a small program on paper first and predicting exactly what it is going to print.

curriculum.title: Level 4 · Lists, Words and Handy Tools
topics: Collecting several items in a list and printing them out one at a time with a loop.
Adding, removing and counting items so that a shopping list can grow and shrink.
Picking an item by its position and learning why Python starts counting at zero.
Joining and splitting words to build sentences and play simple word games.
Choosing a random number or a random item so the game feels different every single time.
Writing a small function of your own and calling it whenever that job needs doing again.
Bringing in a ready-made helper from Python's library, such as random or time.
Turning a block you have copied out three times into one tidy loop or function.

curriculum.title: Level 5 · Your First Finished Projects
topics: Planning a small project by writing down everything it should do before you start coding.
Building a number-guessing game that gives higher and lower hints until the player wins.
Making a quiz that asks several questions and then reports a final score out of ten.
Creating a simple calculator that totals a rupee bill for a pretend shop.
Drawing a turtle scene that changes according to what the user types in.
Testing your project on a friend or a parent and fixing anything they found confusing.
Tidying your code with clear names and short comments so that somebody else can read it.
Presenting your finished project to your tutor and explaining how each part of it works.

short_description: Gentle live Python classes for first-time young coders, built around turtle drawings and small games.
description: Start coding with Python through live sessions, assignments, and mentor feedback.

name: Robotics & Computational Thinking
subtitle: Playful live coaching for younger learners in step-by-step thinking, patterns and algorithms, unplugged and on screen.

curriculum.title: Thinking in Small Steps
topics: Discovering that every big task, such as making a sandwich, can be split into smaller steps done in a fixed order.
Breaking a daily routine like getting ready for school into a picture sequence of separate actions.
Playing partner games where one child gives instructions and the other follows them exactly as spoken.
Spotting the missing step when a set of instructions does not produce the result everybody expected.
Sorting a jumbled set of instruction cards back into a sensible working order.
Describing what a lift or a traffic signal does as a short list of simple repeated steps.
Drawing a first flow of steps on paper, using arrows to show clearly what happens next.

curriculum.title: Finding Patterns
topics: Spotting repeating patterns in beads, tiles, rangoli designs and number sequences and predicting what comes next.
Explaining the rule behind a pattern in words so a friend can continue it without ever seeing the original.
Grouping objects by shared features and noticing which of those features actually matter for the grouping.
Comparing two similar puzzles and reusing the solution from the first to solve the second much faster.
Finding the repeated part inside a long set of instructions and marking it as one section instead of many lines.
Shortening a written plan by replacing that repeated section with a single instruction to do it again.
Creating an original pattern challenge and testing whether a classmate can work out the hidden rule.

curriculum.title: Keeping Only What Matters
topics: Learning that a good plan hides unnecessary detail and keeps only the information needed to act.
Drawing a simple map of a classroom or a park that shows the route without every small object along it.
Deciding which details of a story or a problem can safely be ignored when writing instructions for it.
Naming a group of steps with a single label so the whole group can be called by that name later.
Building a personal set of named actions, such as move, turn and wait, that can be reused in many plans.
Comparing a detailed photograph with a simple icon and discussing why symbols are quicker to follow.
Explaining a familiar game to a younger child using only the rules that genuinely matter.

curriculum.title: Writing Algorithms
topics: Writing a clear step-by-step algorithm that guides a partner across a floor grid to a target square.
Adding decision points so a plan responds differently when something is or is not in the way.
Using counted repetition so an action happens a set number of times without rewriting the same line.
Comparing two different algorithms for the same task and judging which is shorter or more reliable.
Following an algorithm exactly as written to discover where it goes wrong, then correcting that step.
Rebuilding the same algorithm in a block-based coding tool and watching a screen character carry it out.
Using event blocks so an action begins only when a key is pressed or a character is touched.
Recording the finished algorithm in both words and blocks to compare the two ways of writing it.

curriculum.title: Testing, Debugging and Simple Robots
topics: Predicting what a set of blocks will do before running it, then checking that prediction against the result.
Finding and fixing a fault by testing one small section of a plan at a time.
Programming a floor robot or an on-screen turtle to trace squares, triangles and simple letter shapes.
Using sensor blocks so an on-screen robot reacts when it meets a wall or a change of colour.
Storing a number in a variable, such as a score or a step count, and changing it as the plan runs.
Explaining out loud what each part of a plan does, which is the habit that catches most mistakes early.
Improving a working plan so it uses fewer blocks and reads more easily for somebody else.

curriculum.title: My First Computational Project
topics: Choosing a small everyday problem at home or school that a good set of instructions could solve.
Breaking the chosen problem into parts and deciding sensibly which part to build first.
Sketching the plan on paper, including the decisions and the repetitions it will need.
Building the project in a block-based tool, adding movement, sound and simple scoring.
Testing the project with a family member and noting every point where they became confused.
Improving the project from that feedback and writing down exactly what changed and why.
Presenting the finished project to the class and explaining the thinking behind each design choice.
Collecting all the term's projects into a simple portfolio that shows how the thinking grew over time.

short_description: Playful live coaching for younger learners in step-by-step thinking, patterns and algorithms, unplugged and on screen.
description: Build logic and automation skills with beginner robotics concepts and project work.

name: Chess Strategy & Mind Sports
subtitle: Positional understanding, deep calculation and mind-sport training for experienced players.

curriculum.title: Reading a Position: The Language of Strategy
topics: Beginning with no prior study of theory and learning to describe a position in plain words before any judgement is offered.
Breaking any position down into material, king safety, pawn structure, piece activity and control of space.
Separating permanent features such as a ruined pawn structure from temporary ones such as a lead in development.
Recognising a hole as a square that none of your pawns can ever guard again, and treating it as a lasting weakness.
Judging when a knight on a secure central square outclasses a bishop and when the two bishops are the greater long-term asset.
Measuring a space advantage by counting the squares your pawns control in the opponent's half of the board.
Writing a short assessment of a position and then comparing it with an engine's verdict to expose the factors you habitually undervalue.
Summarising the winning plan of a classic strategic game in no more than three sentences of your own.

curriculum.title: Pawn Structures and the Plans They Dictate
topics: Playing both sides of the isolated queen's pawn, attacking with it in one game and blockading firmly against it in the next.
Handling hanging pawns and recognising the precise moment at which one of them should be pushed forward.
Running the minority attack so that the opponent's larger queenside pawn majority is left with a lasting weakness.
Playing pawn chains by striking at the base of the chain rather than battering away at its head.
Understanding why the real play shifts to the wings as soon as the centre becomes locked.
Treating backward, doubled and isolated pawns as targets while making use of the open files they leave behind.
Deciding when to release the central tension and when to keep the opponent guessing for several more moves.
Keeping a notebook of the structures that suit your style and of those you should steer the game away from.

curriculum.title: Calculation, Candidate Moves and Visualisation
topics: Building a disciplined thinking routine that lists the candidate moves before any calculation is begun.
Calculating the forcing continuations first by checking every check, capture and threat in turn.
Training visualisation by calculating four or five moves deep without touching or moving a single piece.
Using the method of comparison to choose between two lines that both look attractive at first glance.
Pruning unpromising branches early instead of recalculating the same variation three times over.
Preventing blunders with a final safety check on the intended move before it is actually played.
Solving demanding studies and composed positions in which the natural first choice is always the wrong one.
Timing calculation exercises so that your accuracy survives genuine pressure from the clock.

curriculum.title: Prophylaxis, Manoeuvring and the Positional Sacrifice
topics: Asking what the opponent intends to do next and preventing it before returning to your own plan.
Restricting an enemy piece patiently until it has no useful square left anywhere on the board.
Regrouping your own pieces over several quiet moves in order to reach a better overall arrangement.
Sacrificing a pawn in return for lasting activity, an open file or a permanent outpost for a knight.
Giving up the exchange in positions where the resulting minor piece completely dominates the opposing rook.
Choosing which pieces to exchange and which to keep when simplifying a favourable position towards the ending.
Playing training games in which the only objective is to improve your worst-placed piece each move.
Studying the endings that arise directly out of your own openings so that every transition is planned in advance.

curriculum.title: Technical Endgames and Conversion
topics: Mastering the Lucena bridge-building win and the Philidor third-rank defence in rook and pawn endings.
Applying the principle that rooks belong behind passed pawns, whether the pawn is yours or the opponent's.
Converting an extra pawn in same-coloured bishop endings, and learning why that same pawn usually fails to win when the bishops run on opposite colours.
Handling knight endings in which zugzwang and a single tempo count for more than raw material.
Deciding when to trade into a queen ending and when the heavy pieces are far better kept on the board.
Defending inferior endings actively rather than sitting passively and waiting to be squeezed to death.
Practising fortress set-ups that hold a draw even when a whole piece down.
Testing every technique by playing the same ending from both sides against the coach.

curriculum.title: Match Preparation, Mind Sports and Strategic Mastery
topics: Preparing for a named opponent by studying their recent games and choosing a move order that leads them away from familiar ground.
Managing sleep, meals and rest between rounds so that the last game of a long event is played as well as the first.
Deciding your tournament strategy when the standings demand a win, or only a draw, in the final round.
Playing long training games and annotating them by hand in words and variations before an engine is ever opened.
Holding an uncomfortable position for hours without drifting into a careless move out of sheer impatience.
Carrying the same candidate-move discipline into draughts and Go, where territory and tempo replace checkmate as the goal.
Testing pattern recognition under time pressure in speed puzzle-solving formats, where a position must be judged in seconds.
Presenting an annotated portfolio of your finest strategic games with all the commentary written in your own words.

short_description: Positional understanding, deep calculation and mind-sport training for experienced players.
description: Structured chess coaching focused on openings, tactics, and tournament readiness.

name: Violin/Viola Lessons for Beginners
subtitle: Gentle live beginner lessons on violin or viola, with no previous experience needed.

curriculum.title: Your First Weeks with the Instrument
topics: Trying both the violin and the viola and choosing the one that suits your reach and the sound you prefer.
Opening and closing the case safely, tightening and loosening the bow hair, and applying rosin without overdoing it.
Finding a relaxed standing and sitting position in which the shoulders, jaw and neck stay free of tension.
Shaping the bow hold on a pencil first and then carrying exactly the same shape across to the bow itself.
Naming the four strings of your chosen instrument and plucking them in order until you can hear which is which.
Drawing your first long bow strokes on an open string and listening for a clean, steady sound with no scratch.
Clapping and counting four-beat rhythms out loud before you try to play any of them.
Playing a short rhythm on open strings with your tutor, starting and stopping at the same moment.

curriculum.title: Left Hand and First Notes
topics: Placing the first, second and third fingers on the fingerboard, using guide tapes as a reference to begin with.
Curving the left-hand fingers over the string so that the fingertips press cleanly without squeezing the neck.
Playing three-note and four-note tunes on one string, and then joining two strings together within the same tune.
Reading the treble clef if you have chosen the violin, or the alto clef if you have chosen the viola.
Recognising crotchets, minims and quavers on the page and counting them aloud as you play them.
Checking each stopped note against the open string beside it to hear whether it is in tune.
Playing a one-octave major scale slowly with a separate bow for every note, in D major on the violin or G major on the viola.
Building a short daily practice habit of around fifteen focused minutes at the same time each day.

curriculum.title: Bowing, Tuning and Simple Tunes
topics: Watching in a mirror to keep the bow travelling parallel to the bridge from the frog all the way to the tip.
Crossing between two neighbouring strings smoothly, without brushing the string that sits between them.
Playing two notes in one bow, and then four notes, to learn your first slurs.
Tuning your own instrument with the fine tuners and a simple electronic tuner before every practice session.
Adding the fourth finger and comparing its pitch with the open string above it until the two match.
Playing easy folk and traditional melodies from the page without stopping at every bar line.
Playing softly and loudly by changing bow speed and weight rather than by pressing harder into the string.
Joining your tutor in echo and call-and-response games that build listening as much as technique.

curriculum.title: Two Strings, Two Keys, First Pieces
topics: Playing one-octave scales and arpeggios in two easy keys across a pair of strings.
Moving the second finger up or down by a semitone and hearing how the character of the tune changes with it.
Adding short detached and staccato strokes near the middle of the bow for a livelier, more articulate sound.
Reading dotted rhythms and rests without losing your sense of the underlying pulse.
Sight-reading four to eight bars of unfamiliar music at a slow, comfortable tempo.
Playing simple duets with your tutor and staying together from the first bar to the last.
Learning three short contrasting pieces securely enough to play them from memory as well as from the page.
Answering easy aural questions, such as clapping back a rhythm or saying whether a phrase rose or fell.

curriculum.title: Your First Performance
topics: Choosing three short pieces of contrasting mood to make up a small programme of your own.
Polishing each piece slowly, section by section, until you can play it through without stumbles.
Playing straight through from start to finish without stopping to correct small mistakes on the way.
Practising walking on, bowing to the audience and settling yourself before the first note.
Managing nerves with a simple breathing exercise and a warm-up routine that you always follow.
Recording a video of your programme at home and watching it back with your tutor to choose two things to improve.
Performing live to family or in an online student showcase arranged by your tutor.
Deciding what to learn next and, if you wish, working towards an entry-level graded exam such as Trinity's Initial Grade.

short_description: Gentle live beginner lessons on violin or viola, with no previous experience needed.
description: Beginner-friendly violin and viola classes with technique drills and repertoire guidance.

👉 Soprano Ukulele is strongly recommended for beginners

🎵 About Ukulele vs Guitar (Short Understanding)

The ukulele is a small, four-stringed instrument originally from Hawaii, traditionally strung with nylon strings and tuned G-C-E-A.

The guitar is a larger six-stringed instrument available in acoustic, classical, and electric variants, with a wider range of tones.

The ukulele offers a lighter, cheerful tone and is generally easier for young beginners, while the guitar provides a broader tonal range and greater repertoire depth.

topics: Recording a multi-track song on the onboard sequencer, building it up one instrument part at a time.
Quantising, punching in and editing recorded tracks to correct timing slips and wrong notes.
Programming a custom drum pattern and bass line for songs where no preset style quite fits.
Mixing track volumes, panning and effect levels so every layer sits clearly in the finished balance.
Connecting the keyboard to a computer or tablet over MIDI and recording into notation or sequencing software.
Taking a pad, bass or lead role within an ensemble and leaving space for the other players.
Improvising a solo over a looping style using notes drawn from the pentatonic and blues scales.
Producing a finished backing track that a singer or instrumentalist can comfortably perform over.

curriculum.title: Live Performance Mastery and Portfolio
topics: Programming a full set list so that each song loads from a saved registration at a single button press.
Setting up a live rig with amplification, stand height, sustain pedal and tidy cable runs before a show.
Sound checking in a hall or studio and adjusting the master equalisation to suit the room.
Sustaining a thirty-minute set with confident links and spoken introductions between songs.
Recovering from mistakes on stage by staying in tempo and rejoining rather than stopping to restart.
Rehearsing to a click so that live tempo stays reliable when adrenaline pushes the pulse forward.
Filming and mixing a studio-quality video of two contrasting arrangements for a personal portfolio.
Preparing a Grade 5 standard examination programme covering technical work and supporting tests.

short_description: Live electronic keyboard classes covering voices, styles, auto-accompaniment and arranging.

name: Drums
subtitle: Personalised live drum kit coaching, from your first groove to the Grade 5 standard.

curriculum.title: Level 1 – Getting Started on the Drum Kit
topics: Arranging the snare, hi-hat, bass drum and cymbals so that every drum falls within easy reach of your arms and feet.
Sitting with a balanced posture at a throne height that lets both heels drop naturally onto the pedals.
Holding the sticks in matched grip with a relaxed fulcrum, letting each stick rebound freely off the head.
Playing single strokes evenly between the right and left hand on a practice pad before moving to the kit.
Counting crotchets and quavers aloud while playing along with a metronome at a slow, comfortable tempo.
Playing your first rock beat, with the bass drum on beats one and three and the snare on beats two and four.
Learning the name and sound of each drum and cymbal, and how the hi-hat pedal opens and closes the two cymbals.
Starting and stopping together with your teacher after a spoken four-beat count-in.

curriculum.title: Level 2 – Reading Rhythm and Playing in Time
topics: Reading drum notation on a five-line stave and identifying which line or space stands for each drum and cymbal.
Counting and playing crotchet, quaver and semiquaver rhythms while keeping the underlying pulse steady.
Building eight-bar grooves in four-four time and repeating them without drifting faster or slower.
Adding simple one-bar fills around the snare and toms and landing cleanly back on beat one.
Playing the double stroke roll slowly, so the second stroke of each pair bounces at the same volume as the first.
Working the bass drum pedal with a relaxed heel-up stroke and an even volume from note to note.
Playing along with a backing track and locking to the click instead of rushing ahead of it.
Preparing two short contrasting pieces to the standard expected at an entry-level graded rock and pop examination.

curriculum.title: Level 3 – Rudiments, Fills and Groove Vocabulary
topics: Practising the single paradiddle and moving its right-left-right-right sticking pattern around the kit.
Playing flams cleanly, keeping a small and consistent gap between the grace note and the main stroke.
Building four-bar fills that run semiquavers across the snare and both toms without losing the pulse.
Opening the hi-hat for an accent and closing it neatly on the following beat.
Marking the start of a new section with a crash cymbal struck on beat one.
Controlling dynamics from soft ghost notes on the snare through to firmly accented backbeats.
Performing a piece with a written intro, verse, chorus and ending by following the road map on the page.
Practising at a range of tempi and noticing exactly where your timing begins to drift.

curriculum.title: Level 4 – Semiquaver Grooves and Style Study
topics: Playing semiquaver hi-hat patterns with a relaxed wrist and even spacing between the notes.
Learning the shuffle feel and playing a blues groove over a triplet-based, swung pulse.
Playing funk grooves that combine syncopated bass drum placements with snare ghost notes.
Building limb independence by holding a steady hi-hat while the bass drum pattern changes underneath it.
Playing in three-four and six-eight and feeling the difference between simple and compound time.
Moving the right hand to the ride cymbal and its bell for a brighter texture through a chorus.
Playing a push that anticipates the downbeat by a quaver and then settling straight back into the groove.
Working a short groove out by ear from a recording and writing it down in drum notation.

curriculum.title: Level 5 – Advanced Coordination and Band Playing
topics: Playing triplet-based fills and moving smoothly between quaver, triplet and semiquaver subdivisions.
Practising the triple paradiddle and the single drag tap and taking both around the full kit.
Playing a swung jazz ride pattern while comping with the snare and bass drum underneath it.
Trying traditional grip for jazz playing and comparing how it feels against your usual matched grip.
Counting your way accurately through a change of time signature in the middle of a piece.
Holding a click track steady while the bass or guitar part shifts underneath you.
Improvising a short solo over an eight-bar structure and landing back on the top of the form.
Setting up band cues such as stops, hits and fills that signal a section change to the rest of the group.

curriculum.title: Level 6 – Grade 5 Standard and Live Performance
topics: Preparing a balanced three-song programme and rehearsing it end to end without stopping.
Playing the technical work expected at the Grade 5 standard, combining rudiments with grooves across the whole kit.
Sight-reading an unseen eight-bar groove and fill at a steady tempo.
Identifying style, time signature and rhythmic figures in aural tests played back to you.
Playing fast fills and pushed accents accurately at the tempo of the original recording.
Managing nerves and stage presence through a full run-through in front of an audience.
Recording a clean take of each song and choosing the strongest ones for a performance portfolio.
Designing a weekly practice routine that balances rudiments, grooves and repertoire so progress continues after the course.

short_description: Personalised live drum kit coaching, from your first groove to the Grade 5 standard.

name: Violin
subtitle: Live one-to-one Western violin coaching, from your first bow stroke to recital and audition standard.

curriculum.title: Foundations of the Violin
topics: Setting the instrument up at the start of each lesson, tightening the bow hair to about a pencil's width and applying rosin evenly along its length.
Building a relaxed playing posture with a chin rest and shoulder rest fitted to your own neck length and frame.
Learning the bow hold with a curved thumb resting against the frog and rounded fingers that leave the wrist free to move.
Drawing long, straight bow strokes parallel to the bridge on each open string, travelling from the frog to the tip and back again.
Naming and tuning the four open strings to G, D, A and E, using the fine tuners for small corrections and the pegs only with your tutor.
Reading the treble clef, note values and simple time signatures well enough to follow a beginner's line without stopping.
Placing the first, second and third fingers in the first-position frame, using guide tapes at first and then listening for the note instead.
Playing short folk-style melodies on the D and A strings with a separate bow for every note and a steady pulse throughout.

curriculum.title: First Position and Reading
topics: Playing one-octave major scales and their arpeggios across two strings with an even tone from the first note to the last.
Coordinating string crossings so the bow arm changes level early and never catches the neighbouring string.
Using the fourth finger in place of the ringing open string so that a legato line keeps the same colour all the way through.
Distinguishing the high and low second finger so that whole steps and half steps land accurately in every key you play.
Practising detache and slurred bowing patterns of two and four notes, dividing the bow so that you do not run out at the tip.
Counting quavers, dotted rhythms and simple syncopation aloud before you attempt to play any of them.
Sight-reading eight-bar passages in D, A and G major at a slow tempo you can hold from beginning to end.
Preparing three short contrasting pieces to the standard expected at Trinity College London's Initial Grade for violin.

curriculum.title: Tone, Rhythm and Early Grade Repertoire
topics: Controlling tone by adjusting bow speed, bow weight and the contact point between the bridge and the fingerboard.
Adding martele and staccato strokes for crisp, articulate note beginnings and clean endings.
Playing two-octave scales and arpeggios in the flat keys and listening for even intonation as the hand crosses strings.
Working with a metronome to build a passage from a slow practice tempo up to performance speed in measured steps.
Shaping phrases with graded dynamics and matching bow distribution to the length of each phrase.
Playing two-part duets with the tutor, taking the upper line and tuning your thirds and sixths against it.
Training the ear to recognise intervals, major and minor tonality and rhythms clapped back to you.
Keeping a practice diary that breaks each week's work into short daily sessions with one clear aim for each.

curriculum.title: Shifting, Vibrato and the Middle Grades
topics: Shifting cleanly into third position with a light guiding thumb and a released left hand that travels as a single unit.
Learning the third-position finger pattern and finding notes by ear as confidently as you find them by sight.
Developing vibrato through wrist-rocking exercises on a stopped note before applying it to sustained notes in repertoire.
Playing three-octave major scales and dominant seventh arpeggios, letting the finger spacing narrow as the hand climbs the fingerboard.
Introducing double stops on adjacent strings and tuning each interval against a sustained drone.
Studying a concert etude that isolates one technical problem, such as string crossing, bow distribution or the accuracy of a shift.
Interpreting Baroque and Classical style, including lighter detache bowing and well-placed ornaments such as trills and appoggiaturas.
Recording your own playing and reviewing it critically against the interpretation you had intended.

curriculum.title: Advanced Technique and Style
topics: Moving fluently through first, second, third, fourth and fifth positions within a single phrase, in scales and in repertoire alike.
Adding spiccato near the balance point and faster sautille closer to the middle of the bow, letting the stick's own spring do the work.
Playing three-octave melodic and harmonic minor scales with their arpeggios from memory and at a steady tempo.
Refining vibrato width and speed so that it suits Baroque, Romantic and twentieth-century writing rather than staying the same throughout.
Sustaining double stops and three-note chords by rolling the bow across the strings instead of pressing through them.
Learning an extended sonata or concerto movement and organising it into manageable practice sections with separate goals.
Sight-reading at the standard of a grade below your working level, including changes of key, metre and position.
Analysing the harmony and form of what you play so that your phrasing follows the structure of the music.

curriculum.title: Recital, Audition and Portfolio
topics: Building a balanced recital programme of contrasting periods, keys and characters that fits a set playing time.
Memorising a full movement and rehearsing safe recovery points so that a slip never stops the performance.
Rehearsing with a piano accompaniment track and matching your entries, your rubato and your final chords to it.
Managing performance nerves with breathing exercises, a fixed warm-up routine and practice at walking on and beginning.
Running complete exam-style sessions covering scales, pieces, sight-reading and aural work under time pressure.
Recording a polished video portfolio of contrasting movements suitable for school auditions or conservatoire applications.
Leading a line in an ensemble, giving a clear preparatory gesture and matching the tuning and bowing of the players around you.
Setting your own long-term practice goals and looking after the instrument, strings, bow and bridge between lessons.

short_description: Live one-to-one Western violin coaching, from your first bow stroke to recital and audition standard.

name: Veena
subtitle: Personalised live Saraswati veena coaching in the Carnatic tradition, from first varisai to the concert stage.

curriculum.title: Level 1 – Meeting the Veena
topics: Sitting with the kudam resting on the lap and the dandi angled so the left hand reaches the frets easily.
Learning the names of the parts, including the kudam, the dandi, the twenty-four frets, the four main strings and the three side strings.
Wearing the wire plectra on the index and middle fingers of the right hand and plucking with a light wrist.
Tuning the four main strings in the standard Sa-Pa-Sa-Pa relationship at your chosen shruti, checking each one against a drone.
Pressing the string down onto the fret with the fingertip so that each swara sounds clean and free of buzz.
Plucking single swaras and letting each one ring for its full length before sounding the next.
Singing and then playing the seven swaras in ascending and descending order.
Keeping Adi tala by counting the beats aloud while you play slow, evenly spaced swaras.

curriculum.title: Level 2 – Varisai Foundations
topics: Playing the sarali varisai in the first, second and third speeds with even plucking throughout.
Alternating index and middle plectrum strokes so that no stroke is louder than the one beside it.
Playing janta varisai with firm paired strokes on each repeated swara.
Strumming the three side strings with the little finger to close a phrase in tala.
Practising dhatu varisai patterns that leap between swaras which are not next to each other.
Counting Adi tala and Rupaka tala with the standard hand gestures while you play.
Working through the sapta tala alankaram exercises across the seven basic talas.
Finding each swara position on the frets by feel, without looking down at the left hand.

curriculum.title: Level 3 – Geetham and the First Ragas
topics: Playing simple geetham compositions from memory with the tala held steady from beginning to end.
Introducing the jaaru gamaka by gliding the finger smoothly up and down between two frets.
Producing gamakas by pulling the string sideways across the fret to raise the pitch without plucking again.
Understanding how a raga is defined by its arohana and avarohana, the ascending and descending order of its swaras.
Playing pieces in two contrasting ragas and hearing what gives each one its own character.
Holding the correct laya when a composition moves up into the second speed.
Explaining terms such as swara, arohana, avarohana, tala and avartana in your own words.
Preparing a two-item recital to the standard of a junior certificate examination in Carnatic music.

curriculum.title: Level 4 – Swarajathi and Varnam
topics: Playing swarajathi compositions that set passages of swaras against lines of sahitya.
Working through an Adi tala varnam in both the first and the second speed.
Refining the kampita gamaka with a controlled oscillation around a single fret.
Playing across two sthayis and shifting the left hand smoothly between the registers.
Shaping phrases so that the veena carries the contour of a singing voice, as the sahitya itself would be sung.
Playing against a tambura drone and adjusting your intonation to it continuously.
Understanding the structure of a varnam, from the pallavi and anupallavi through the muktayi swara to the charanam swaras.
Reciting the notation of a new piece aloud in swara syllables before attempting it on the instrument.

curriculum.title: Level 5 – Kritis and Manodharma
topics: Learning kritis complete with their pallavi, anupallavi and charanam sections.
Playing a short raga alapana without tala, shaping and sustaining each phrase freely on the main strings.
Developing tanam by weaving rhythmic strokes on the side strings between the melodic phrases.
Improvising kalpana swaras that resolve accurately onto the eduppu of the composition.
Playing neraval by varying a single line of sahitya across several avartanas.
Handling the uneven cycles of Misra Chapu and Khanda Chapu alongside the even count of Adi tala.
Studying the characteristic phrases that let a listener recognise a major raga within a few notes.
Discussing the style and language of the major Carnatic composers whose compositions you are learning.

curriculum.title: Level 6 – Kutcheri Preparation and Portfolio
topics: Building a balanced kutcheri list that opens with a varnam and closes with lighter tukkada items.
Rehearsing with a mridangam accompanist, giving clear cues and leaving room for the tani avartanam.
Presenting a main item with extended alapana, neraval and kalpana swara improvisation.
Retuning quickly and confidently on stage between items without losing the attention of the audience.
Managing seating, posture and microphone placement so that the veena carries in a live hall.
Recording a full-length concert set as a portfolio for auditions and sabha applications.
Preparing for a senior graded certificate examination in Carnatic music, including its written theory paper.
Setting out a daily sadhakam routine that keeps varisai, gamaka work and repertoire equally fresh.

short_description: Personalised live Saraswati veena coaching in the Carnatic tradition, from first varisai to the concert stage.

name: Cello
subtitle: Personalised live cello coaching, from open strings to the Grade 5 standard.

curriculum.title: Level 1 – First Steps on the Cello
topics: Adjusting the endpin so that the instrument sits at the right height for your body.
Sitting forward on the chair with the cello resting gently against your chest and knees.
Naming the four open strings, C, G, D and A, and plucking them pizzicato with a relaxed right hand.
Building a rounded bow hold with a flexible thumb and naturally curved fingers.
Drawing the bow in a straight line parallel to the bridge on each open string.
Placing the left-hand fingers in first position with a rounded hand shape and no squeezing of the neck.
Reading notes in the bass clef and matching each one to a finger on a particular string.
Playing simple two-note and three-note tunes while your teacher plays a supporting part.

curriculum.title: Level 2 – First Position and Basic Bowing
topics: Playing one-octave scales and arpeggios in first position with an even tone from note to note.
Using detache strokes with a consistent bow speed and a steady contact point between bridge and fingerboard.
Crossing between adjacent strings smoothly without catching the string in between.
Counting rests accurately and holding long notes for their full written value.
Playing at two clear dynamic levels and hearing how bow weight and speed change the volume.
Learning the extension that widens the space between the first and second fingers by a semitone to reach a note outside the hand position.
Tuning the cello with the fine tuners, matching each string to a drone or to a piano note.
Preparing short contrasting pieces to the standard of an Initial grade examination.

curriculum.title: Level 3 – Slurs, Keys and Playing with Others
topics: Playing slurred pairs, and then longer slurred groups, within a single bow stroke.
Learning scales and arpeggios in several major and minor keys across one and two octaves.
Reading key signatures and adjusting your finger placement for the sharps or flats they carry.
Playing duets and listening across to match your intonation and timing to your partner's.
Reading eight bars of easy music at sight, checking the key and time signature before you begin.
Practising short studies that isolate one technical problem at a time.
Playing in three-four, four-four and six-eight and feeling how differently each metre moves.
Preparing a balanced three-piece programme for a graded examination.

curriculum.title: Level 4 – Shifting and Tone
topics: Shifting up into fourth position and back down to first without losing the intonation.
Keeping the thumb behind the neck as a reference point so that every shift lands in the same place.
Introducing vibrato as a small rolling motion driven by a relaxed forearm.
Contrasting staccato and legato passages within the same piece of music.
Using the whole length of the bow and controlling the change of direction at both the tip and the heel.
Playing passages that travel through second and third position across a wider range.
Working out sensible fingerings for a new piece before playing it through.
Performing from memory a piece you have prepared over several weeks.

curriculum.title: Level 5 – Expressive Playing
topics: Varying the width and speed of the vibrato to suit the mood of a phrase.
Shaping a phrase so that it has a clear beginning, a high point and a settled ending.
Reading tenor clef when the music climbs above the bass stave, and switching between the two clefs mid-piece.
Using spiccato and other off-string strokes at a moderate tempo, letting the bow bounce naturally.
Playing double stops so that both strings speak cleanly and sound in tune together.
Playing dotted and syncopated rhythms accurately, checking them against a slow metronome.
Preparing repertoire from contrasting periods and adjusting your bowing and vibrato to suit each style.
Rehearsing with piano accompaniment, following the pianist's cues while holding your own line.

curriculum.title: Level 6 – Grade 5 Standard and Recital Skills
topics: Playing the full set of scales, arpeggios and studies required at the Grade 5 standard in both major and minor keys.
Performing a three-piece programme straight through, carrying on rather than stopping for small slips.
Sight-reading unfamiliar music at the Grade 5 standard after only a short look at the page.
Answering aural tests by singing back a short phrase and describing what changed on a second playing.
Tuning independently with the pegs as well as the fine tuners, and keeping the instrument in order by rosining the bow and fitting a replacement string.
Walking on, settling on the chair and acknowledging the audience as part of a recital.
Recording yourself and listening back critically for intonation, tone quality and rhythmic accuracy.
Planning a personal practice routine, spread across the week, that carries you towards Grade 6 and beyond.

short_description: Personalised live cello coaching, from open strings to the Grade 5 standard.

name: Viola
subtitle: Live one-to-one viola tuition, from the alto clef and the C string to chamber and recital playing.

curriculum.title: Meeting the Viola
topics: Choosing a viola measured in inches rather than in the fractions used for violins, so the left hand reaches the fourth finger without strain.
Supporting a larger, heavier instrument with a well-fitted shoulder rest and a posture balanced through the back rather than the neck.
Holding the heavier viola bow so that its extra weight sinks into the string of its own accord instead of being pressed in.
Tuning the four strings to C, G, D and A, and hearing the low C sound a fifth below the violin's lowest string.
Reading the alto clef from the very first lesson, with middle C sitting on the centre line of the stave.
Drawing full, even bows on each open string and listening for a warm, unforced sound rather than a bright one.
Setting a first-position left-hand frame with wider finger spacing than a violinist uses, keeping every finger curved over the string.
Playing short melodies on the D and A strings while naming each note aloud in the alto clef as you go.

curriculum.title: First Position Fluency
topics: Playing one-octave major scales and arpeggios in C, G and D across a pair of strings with a matched tone.
Crossing between the C and G strings without a scratchy attack, preparing the arm level before the note arrives.
Drawing sound from the lower strings with a slower bow and more weight, since the thicker strings need longer to speak.
Stretching the fourth finger accurately on the longer viola string length and checking it against the open string above.
Slurring two, three and four notes in one bow while the left hand keeps working independently of the bow arm.
Reading dotted rhythms, quavers and rests fluently in the alto clef at a moderate tempo.
Naming the key signature and spotting the hardest bar before you begin any piece of sight-reading.
Preparing short contrasting pieces to the standard expected at an initial-level graded string exam.

curriculum.title: Tone and the Inner Voice
topics: Producing a full, resonant tone on the C string by combining bow weight with a slower stroke and a contact point nearer the bridge.
Adding martele and staccato strokes for clear articulation in dance movements and march-like passages.
Playing two-octave scales and arpeggios in the flat keys that viola writing favours, keeping the tone equal across all four strings.
Playing the inner harmony line in duets while the tutor takes the melody, and judging how far to sit underneath it.
Shaping phrases with dynamic shading and planning bow distribution so that you still have bow left at the end of the phrase.
Counting compound time and changes of metre accurately against a metronome without losing the beat.
Hearing from inside a chord whether it is major or minor, and identifying the interval the tutor plays against your held note.
Splitting each practice session into a technical half and a repertoire half, and timing both so that neither is neglected.

curriculum.title: Third Position and Viola Colour
topics: Shifting into third position with a relaxed thumb and an unhurried arm movement that carries the whole hand together.
Learning the third-position finger pattern and reading the treble clef passages that appear once the writing climbs.
Building a warm viola vibrato with a slightly wider and slower oscillation than a violinist would use.
Playing two-octave and then three-octave scales with even intonation across the wider viola fingerboard.
Tuning double stops in thirds and sixths against a sustained drone until the beats between the two notes disappear.
Working through a technical study chosen to target the one weakness your tutor has identified in your playing.
Adapting bow style to Baroque, Classical and Romantic idioms instead of playing everything with the same stroke.
Listening back to a recording of your own practice and marking the bars where the tone or the tuning fell away.

curriculum.title: Advanced Technique and Chamber Playing
topics: Moving confidently from first through to fifth position and back again within a single phrase.
Playing spiccato and controlled off-string strokes on a bow heavy enough to need extra preparation before each bounce.
Playing three-octave melodic and harmonic minor scales from memory, reaching the high positions on the A string cleanly.
Sustaining double stops and three-note chords with a rolled, unhurried bow arm that leaves the lower notes ringing.
Reading fluently in both alto and treble clef and switching between them mid-piece without hesitation.
Learning a substantial sonata or concerto movement from the viola repertoire and working it in structured sections.
Rehearsing chamber parts, counting long rests accurately and coming back in with confidence after them.
Sight-reading just below your working grade, including awkward clef changes and unexpected accidentals.

curriculum.title: Recital, Orchestra and Portfolio
topics: Assembling a contrasting recital programme that shows both your lyrical playing and your more virtuosic work.
Memorising an extended movement and marking safe restart points to use if concentration slips on stage.
Coordinating entries, pauses and final chords with a piano accompaniment track until the two parts breathe together.
Building stage confidence through repeated mock performances, each one played straight through without stopping.
Talking about your programme aloud, explaining the style and structure of each piece as an audition panel may ask you to.
Recording an audition video for a youth orchestra seat, including the orchestral excerpts that panels commonly set for violists.
Preparing an orchestral viola section part, marking bowings to match the section and counting rests from the conductor's beat.
Deciding where to take the viola next, whether towards chamber music, orchestral playing or further graded exams.

short_description: Live one-to-one viola tuition, from the alto clef and the C string to chamber and recital playing.

name: Clarinet
subtitle: Personalised live B flat clarinet lessons, from first sounds to graded examinations and ensemble playing.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Reed, Embouchure and First Sounds
topics: Wetting a reed and setting it level with the tip of the mouthpiece, then hearing how a hair's difference in placement changes the response.
Forming an embouchure with a flat chin, firm corners and the lower lip cushioning the reed against the lower teeth.
Sounding the mouthpiece and barrel alone and holding that pitch steadily before playing on the whole instrument.
Playing the first notes of the chalumeau register, the low and woody range in which a clarinettist begins.
Covering the open tone holes with the flat pads of the fingers so that every note speaks without a gurgle.
Reading treble-clef notation and clapping each rhythm before transferring it to the instrument.
Blowing a long, level note on a warm, fast air stream and listening for any waver in pitch or volume.
Understanding that the B flat clarinet sounds a tone lower than written, which is why its part is printed a tone higher than it sounds.

curriculum.title: Level 2 — The Chalumeau Register and Rhythm
topics: Sealing the open tone holes completely and at speed so that notes never squeak or half-speak.
Improving the thin, stuffy throat tones by adding resonance fingerings in the right hand below.
Playing one-octave major scales and their arpeggios smoothly and from memory.
Starting notes with the tip of the tongue touching the tip of the reed lightly rather than slapping at it.
Holding long tones for a steady count while keeping both pitch and volume level throughout.
Reading simple and compound time signatures and counting rests accurately while another part plays.
Preparing first-grade pieces that stay within the chalumeau register, before the break is introduced.
Taking the lower line of a two-part arrangement with the teacher and listening to the harmony above.

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Crossing the Break
topics: Using the register key under the left thumb to move from the chalumeau into the clarion register, where the pitch rises by a twelfth rather than an octave.
Practising slow slurs across the break until the change of register can no longer be heard.
Putting the right-hand fingers down in advance so that the most awkward crossings arrive smoothly.
Playing two-octave scales that pass through the break with no gap or bump in the sound.
Tracing a squeak back to its cause, whether it is embouchure pressure, a leaking finger or a tired reed.
Controlling soft playing so that a quiet note holds its pitch instead of thinning or dropping out.
Sight-reading unfamiliar lines and scanning ahead for accidentals and break crossings before they arrive.
Building a programme of contrasting styles at about third-grade standard.

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Clarion Register and Articulation
topics: Producing a full, focused clarion tone with an open throat and fast, well-supported air.
Practising staccato so that notes are short and pointed but never clipped or airless.
Playing chromatic scales fluently and using the side and sliver keys as alternatives at the awkward joins.
Learning minor scales in both harmonic and melodic forms across two octaves.
Comparing how phrasing differs between a classical study and a lighter folk-derived piece.
Tuning to an accompaniment by pulling slightly at the barrel and then refining the pitch with the embouchure.
Working through studies chosen to attack particular weaknesses in finger work and articulation.
Preparing an examination programme at roughly fifth-grade standard, including the supporting tests.

Playing extended scale patterns and arpeggios at performance tempo entirely from memory.
Rehearsing orchestral clarinet solos and wind-band parts, counting long rests and entering cold but in tune.
Reading a part written for the A clarinet and understanding why composers ask for that instrument in sharp keys.
Blending inside a clarinet section by matching note length and tone exactly to the player leading it.
Recognising that classical clarinet playing is normally shaped without vibrato, unlike flute and saxophone playing.
Interpreting jazz, klezmer and light-music writing, where bends, slides and a warmer inflection are expected.
Playing the bass clarinet and adapting the air and embouchure to a much larger reed while the fingering stays familiar.

topics: Preparing a recital programme of contrasting periods and memorising one substantial movement.
Rehearsing with a pianist and balancing a quiet clarinet line against an open piano lid.
Recording performances and listening back for evenness of tone from the chalumeau through to the altissimo.
Preparing higher-grade scale requirements across the full working range, from the lowest written E upwards, from memory.
Keeping the breath low and the throat open when nerves shorten the air, so that the tone does not thin on the platform.
Choosing a warm-up that settles the embouchure and the fingers without tiring the lip before a performance.
Reading an unseen orchestral or band part at an audition and holding a steady pulse under pressure.
Putting together an audition file of recordings spanning an orchestral-style solo, a study and a lighter piece.

Producing the open dayan bols na and tin so that the drum rings on freely after the stroke

Sounding the open ghe on the bayan and using the heel of the hand to bend its pitch
Combining both drums so that dha and dhin sound as single unified strokes rather than two separate ones

Raising the speed of a kaida in stages while keeping every bol clearly audible
Reciting a complete kaida with all its paltas from memory before playing it on the drums

Keeping a rela smooth and unbroken as the tempo gradually rises
Opening a solo with a peshkar that develops the theka slowly and expansively
Playing chakradar compositions in which a complete phrase repeats three times to arrive on sam

name: Indian Flute
subtitle: Live one-to-one bansuri coaching in the Hindustani tradition, from the first swara to a full raag recital.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — First Breath and the Seven Swaras
topics: Sitting cross-legged with a straight back and the bansuri angled out to the right, keeping the shoulders loose and free of strain.
Directing a thin, steady stream of air across the far edge of the mukharandhra, the blowing hole, until a clear tone appears.
Sealing the six finger holes with the soft pads of the fingers rather than the tips, so that no air leaks at the edges.
Playing Sa with the top three holes closed and matching it to a tanpura drone until the note settles perfectly in tune.
Sounding the seven shuddha swaras of the madhya saptak in order and holding each one steady for a full breath.
Breathing low and evenly from the diaphragm so that a swara can be sustained without the pitch wobbling.
Singing each swara aloud before playing it, so that the ear leads the fingers from the very first lesson.
Reading and reciting sargam, the swara notation in which Hindustani compositions are written down and memorised.

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Alankars, Paltas and the Three Saptaks
topics: Moving between mandra, madhya and taar saptak by changing the speed and pressure of the breath while the fingering stays the same.
Working through ascending and descending alankars until the fingers travel through them without hesitation.
Finding the komal swaras by half-covering the holes and checking each flattened pitch against the tanpura.
Placing tivra madhyam accurately and hearing how it changes the colour of a phrase.
Practising palta patterns at three different speeds so that clarity survives as the tempo rises.
Clapping the tali and khali of teental and landing simple phrases squarely on sam.
Extending breath stamina with long-held swaras, adding a little to the sustained count each week.

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Phukar, Breath Articulation and First Raags
topics: Shaping the breath attack, or phukar, so that a swara can begin softly, firmly or with a sudden accent.

Separating repeated swaras with the breath and with a light strike of the finger on the hole, since bansuri playing shapes phrases this way rather than with the tongued articulation of the Western concert flute.
Learning the aroh and avroh of a first pentatonic raag and identifying its vadi and samvadi.
Exploring the pakad, the short catch-phrase by which a listener recognises a raag.
Playing a slow bandish set in teental and returning cleanly to sam at the end of every cycle.
Practising with a lehra or a tabla accompaniment to build a reliable inner sense of laya.
Telling apart by ear two raags built from the same set of swaras but moving in very different ways.
Learning a composition by listening and repetition, as the tradition is handed down, rather than from a printed part.

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Meend, Gamak and Ornamentation
topics: Producing meend by rolling the fingers gradually off the holes so that one swara glides into the next without a break.
Adding kan swaras as feather-light grace notes that brush a neighbouring pitch and vanish again.
Practising murki, the small, quick cluster of swaras that decorates a resting note.
Playing khatka with more weight and attack than murki so that it gives a phrase a sharp lift.
Controlling andolan, the slow and deliberate oscillation around a swara that gives certain raags their gravity.
Producing gamak as a broad, forceful shake of the swara driven from the breath, quite distinct from the light vibrato of Western wind playing.
Combining two or three ornaments inside a single phrase without losing the underlying laya.

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Alap, Jod and Improvisation
topics: Unfolding a raag slowly in alap without a fixed pulse, letting each swara settle before moving on.
Introducing a steady pulse in jod and building intensity while keeping the tone even and unhurried.
Developing taans, fast runs of swaras, from slow patterns practised against the lehra until they are secure at speed.
Improvising badhat, the gradual phrase-by-phrase expansion of a raag, staying inside the movements the raag permits.
Playing a bandish and returning accurately to the mukhda after every improvised excursion.
Working in taals such as jhaptaal of ten beats and ektaal of twelve, and feeling where their vibhags fall.
Listening closely to recordings of senior artistes and putting into words what makes a phrase effective.
Understanding how the samay chakra, the cycle of times of day and seasons, guides the choice of raag in a recital.

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Recital Craft and Performance
topics: Planning a half-hour recital that moves from alap and jod through a vilambit bandish to a drut conclusion.
Playing jhala passages at speed while keeping the tone round and the breath fully supported.
Rehearsing with a tabla player, giving a clear lead into each tihai and handing the stage over during solo passages.
Moving between bansuris of different lengths so that the tonic suits the raag or a vocalist's Sa.
Recording a complete performance and reviewing tuning against the tanpura, the pacing of the badhat and the joins between sections.
Pacing a programme and settling the nerves so that breath and stamina last through to the final piece.
Introducing each raag to the audience in a sentence or two that conveys its mood and its time.
Building a portfolio of recorded raag performances for cultural festival auditions and university entrance.

What is the difference between Indian Bansuri Flute and Western Concert Flute?

The Bansuri is a bamboo flute without keys, used mainly in Indian classical music, focusing on expressive playing and improvisation.The Western Concert Flute is a metal, key-based instrument (Boehm system) used in Western classical, orchestral, and modern music.Bansuri relies on breath control and finger placement, while the Western flute allows faster, more precise note changes using keys.The sound of the Bansuri is warm and earthy, whereas the Western flute is bright and versatile.Bansuri learning is largely oral, while Western flute follows structured notation and exams (ABRSM, Trinity).Choose Bansuri for Indian classical expression, and Western flute for global music and certifications.

Balancing the flute on three points of contact, the base of the left index finger, the right thumb and the chin, so that the fingers stay free to move.
Playing the first notes of the middle register and holding each one for a steady count without the pitch sagging.
Reading treble-clef pitches and simple rhythms in common time and playing them straight from the page.
Beginning each note with a soft tongued syllable rather than pushing it out with a shove of air.
Breathing in low and quietly through the corners of the mouth so that a short phrase can be finished comfortably.
Playing short five-note tunes by ear as well as from notation, so that the ear and the eye develop side by side.

Working down to the lowest notes of the flute and keeping them warm and centred rather than breathy and unfocused.
Operating the foot-joint keys with the right little finger accurately and at speed.
Playing major scales and their arpeggios over one octave from memory and in a steady pulse.
Tuning by drawing the headjoint out a few millimetres, then correcting smaller errors by changing the direction of the air with the lips.
Reading dotted rhythms, ties and rests confidently in both simple and compound time.
Hearing that the flute sounds at written pitch, unlike the B flat and E flat instruments it often plays alongside.
Preparing short pieces to the standard of an initial or first-grade examination, including the supporting tests.

Playing two-octave major and minor scales evenly against a steady beat.
Developing single tonguing that stays crisp and even as the tempo rises.
Producing harmonics from low fingerings to build flexibility in the embouchure and focus in the sound.
Shaping dynamics from soft to loud while holding the pitch steady with the angle of the air.
Sight-reading short unfamiliar pieces and keeping the pulse moving through any slips.
Adding a gentle vibrato supported from the abdomen, and judging where a phrase is better left plain.
Working towards the technical requirements and repertoire standard of about a third-grade examination.

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Third Octave and Musical Style
topics: Managing the third octave with accurate fingerings and a supported sound that never turns shrill.
Learning double tonguing so that rapid repeated notes stay clean and even.
Practising chromatic scales across the full working range at steadily increasing speeds.
Studying how Baroque, Classical and Romantic writing ask for different articulation, ornamentation and phrasing.
Working through studies that isolate awkward finger crossings and rehearsing them slowly before lifting the tempo.
Playing with a piano accompaniment and adjusting intonation while listening to the harmony underneath.
Interpreting expression markings and choosing where to breathe in a long phrase without breaking its shape.
Preparing a balanced examination programme at around fifth-grade standard, including the aural and sight-reading tests.

topics: Refining intonation across all three registers with a daily long-tone routine checked against a tuner.
Playing scale patterns in thirds and broken chords at performance tempo entirely from memory.
Adding flutter tonguing and harmonic-based colour effects called for in twentieth-century writing.
Rehearsing orchestral flute excerpts, counting long rests and coming in cold on an exposed entry.
Blending in a flute choir or wind ensemble and matching tone and vibrato to the player alongside.
Playing the piccolo and the alto flute and feeling how each changes the demands on the embouchure and the air supply.
Preparing unaccompanied works that expose every weakness in pitch, rhythm and phrasing.

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Recital Preparation and Portfolio
topics: Building a recital programme drawn from contrasting periods and memorising at least one substantial work.
Rehearsing with a pianist and agreeing tempi, cues and page turns well before the performance.
Recording a complete run-through and assessing tone, intonation and musical shaping honestly.
Preparing higher graded examinations with scales and arpeggios played from memory at the required speeds.
Structuring a warm-up and a mental rehearsal that settle the nerves before walking on to the platform.
Writing short programme notes that place each work in its historical context for the audience.
Pacing practice in the final weeks so that the programme peaks on the day rather than a fortnight early.
Assembling an audition portfolio of recordings, a repertoire list and a dated practice log.

Setting the neck strap so that the instrument comes up to the mouth instead of the head reaching down to it.
Forming an embouchure that rests the reed on a cushioned lower lip with even pressure all the way around.

Starting each note with a light touch of the tongue tip against the tip of the reed.

curriculum.title: Level 1: Reading the Stave
topics: Naming notes on the treble and bass staves instantly, without counting up from the bottom line.
Writing note values from the semibreve to the semiquaver together with their matching rests.
Grouping beats correctly in simple time signatures of two, three and four.
Learning how sharps, flats and naturals alter a pitch and how long they last within a bar.
Using ledger lines to write pitches that sit above and below the printed stave.
Marking basic dynamic and tempo terms and explaining what a performer should do about each.
Clapping written rhythms accurately before attempting to sing or play them.

curriculum.title: Level 2: Scales, Keys and Intervals
topics: Building major scales using the correct pattern of tones and semitones.
Writing key signatures up to four sharps and four flats and recognising them at a glance.
Constructing natural, harmonic and melodic minor scales and hearing what separates them.
Pairing every major key with its relative minor and explaining what the two have in common.
Measuring intervals by number and quality, from a minor second up to a perfect octave.
Naming the degrees of the scale as tonic, supertonic, mediant, dominant and the rest.
Transposing a short melody into a new key without altering its melodic shape.
Working in compound time and grouping quavers correctly in six-eight and nine-eight.

curriculum.title: Level 3: Chords, Cadences and Basic Harmony
topics: Building major, minor, diminished and augmented triads from any given root note.
Writing triads in root position, first inversion and second inversion.
Labelling chords with Roman numerals and with the chord symbols used in popular music.
Recognising perfect, imperfect, plagal and interrupted cadences at the close of a phrase.
Harmonising a simple melody using only the tonic, subdominant and dominant chords.
Adding the dominant seventh and hearing why it pulls so strongly back towards the tonic.
Identifying passing notes and other decoration that sits outside the underlying chord.

curriculum.title: Level 4: The Indian Swara System in Context
topics: Naming the seven shuddha swaras and locating them against a chosen tonic rather than a fixed concert pitch.
Understanding the four komal swaras and tivra Madhyam, and how twelve pitches come to fill the octave.
Comparing sargam with movable-doh solfege and noting exactly where the two systems part company.
Explaining shruti as the finer gradations of pitch, counted traditionally as twenty-two, that lie between the named swaras.
Distinguishing the seventy-two melakarta of the Carnatic system from the ten thaats of Hindustani music.
Reading and writing Bhatkhande swaralipi for a short phrase, and noting how Carnatic notation marks tala differently.
Counting an avartan of teentaal, marking sam and khaali, and setting the cycle beside a western time signature.
Discussing why Indian classical music builds on a drone and a single melodic line while western music developed functional harmony.

topics: Identifying binary, ternary, rondo and theme-and-variation structures both by ear and on the page.
Describing texture as monophonic, homophonic or polyphonic using examples drawn from listening.
Reading the alto and tenor clefs well enough to follow a string or choral score.
Recognising orchestral instruments by their written ranges and their transpositions.
Following a short open score and tracking each individual part through a passage.
Explaining ornaments such as trills, mordents and grace notes and writing them out in full.
Analysing how a composer modulates to a related key and then returns home.

curriculum.title: Level 6: Composition, Analysis and Exam Craft
topics: Writing an eight-bar melody with a clear phrase structure and a convincing final cadence.
Setting a short verse of text to music with sensible word stress and workable breathing points.
Harmonising a given melody in four parts while avoiding consecutive fifths and octaves.
Composing a simple keyboard or guitar accompaniment pattern beneath a written tune.
Analysing a complete short piece for its key, structure, harmony and expressive devices.
Answering past-style theory questions under timed conditions to build examination speed.
Preparing systematically for recognised graded theory examinations up to a Grade Five standard.
Presenting a small folio of original compositions with written notes explaining each choice.
