name: Trumpet
subtitle: Personalised live trumpet coaching, from the first buzz to solo and ensemble performance.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Buzzing, Breath and First Notes
topics: Producing a relaxed, breath-driven lip buzz before the mouthpiece is brought to the lips at all.
Placing the mouthpiece comfortably on the lips and holding it lightly enough for the lips to keep vibrating freely.
Taking a full, low breath and releasing it in a steady stream rather than pushing from the throat.
Playing the first sustained notes in the middle range with a warm, unforced sound.
Learning the three valve fingerings and pressing each valve squarely all the way down.
Reading treble-clef notes and simple rhythms and playing them at sight.
Resting for as long as you have just played, so that the lip recovers and the sound never becomes forced.
Hearing that a written C on the B flat trumpet sounds as a concert B flat when checked against a piano.

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Partials, Slurs and Scales
topics: Moving between partials on the same valve combination by changing air speed and lip tension alone.
Practising slow lip slurs to build flexibility between neighbouring harmonics.
Playing one-octave major scales and their arpeggios evenly and from memory.
Beginning notes cleanly with the tongue instead of pushing them in with a surge of air.
Building endurance through short practice blocks separated by proper rest.
Counting simple and compound time signatures and playing dotted rhythms accurately.
Preparing short first-grade pieces chosen to sit comfortably in the middle of the range.
Sharing a melody with the teacher in duets and tuning to the other part with the main tuning slide.

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Range, Tone and Articulation
topics: Extending the range upwards through air support and firmer corners rather than by pressing the mouthpiece harder.
Reaching down into the low register and keeping those notes centred and full.
Developing crisp single tonguing that stays even as the tempo increases.
Playing minor and chromatic scales across the working range from memory.
Pushing the first and third valve slides out to correct the sharpness of combinations such as one-three and one-two-three.
Shaping dynamics from soft to loud while the pitch stays completely steady.
Sight-reading unfamiliar lines and keeping the pulse moving through any difficulty.
Preparing a programme of contrasting styles at about third-grade standard.

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Multiple Tonguing, Mutes and Style
topics: Learning double and triple tonguing so that rapid passages stay clean and even.
Practising flexibility studies that leap across several partials within a single breath.
Playing all the major and minor scales over the required range from memory.
Adapting sound and articulation for orchestral writing, for lighter popular styles and for solo playing with piano.
Playing with straight, cup and harmon mutes and compensating for the way each one pushes the pitch sharp.
Working through studies that target particular weaknesses in range and endurance.
Tuning within a section by listening down to the bass line rather than only to the player alongside.
Preparing a fifth-grade examination programme, choosing pieces that do not all sit in the tiring upper range.

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Ensemble Playing and Doubling
topics: Rehearsing orchestral and concert-band trumpet parts, counting long rests and entering cold and in tune.
Playing the cornet for brass-band work, since the British brass band scores for cornets rather than for trumpets.
Playing the flugelhorn and hearing how its wider conical bore suits a soft, lyrical line.
Leading a section and matching note lengths and attack with the players around you.
Building a daily routine that balances warm-up, flexibility work, technical study and rest.
Improvising simple solos over a blues and over straightforward jazz chord sequences.
Playing lyrical studies that demand long phrases and controlled soft playing at the top of the stave.
Rebuilding the embouchure sensibly after heavy playing or after a break from regular practice.

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Performance and Audition Readiness
topics: Preparing a recital programme of contrasting styles and memorising one substantial work.
Rehearsing with a pianist and agreeing tempi, cues and repeats well in advance of the performance.
Recording performances and reviewing whether the sound stays free and centred in the closing minutes.
Transposing at sight from parts written in C, as orchestral trumpet playing regularly demands.
Pacing a programme, and the warm-up before it, so that lip strength lasts through to the final piece.
Settling stage nerves with a dependable routine of long tones and quiet flexibility work.
Balancing within an ensemble so that a bright trumpet line supports the other parts instead of swamping them.
Gathering audition recordings that show lead playing, a lyrical solo and an orchestral excerpt.

name: Sitar
subtitle: Live one-to-one sitar training in the Hindustani classical tradition.

curriculum.title: Meeting the Sitar
topics: Naming the parts of the sitar and understanding how the tumba gourd, the curved frets and the wide bridge shape its tone
Sitting cross-legged in the traditional posture with the gourd resting on the left foot and the neck angled upwards
Wearing the mizrab on the right index finger and shaping its wire so that it neither pinches nor slips
Striking the baj string with a clean inward da and outward ra and keeping the two strokes perfectly even
Tuning the main baj string and the chikari drone strings to a chosen tonic sa
Understanding what the tarab sympathetic strings do and how they colour every swara that is played
Finding the seven shuddha swaras along the tied frets and singing each one while playing it
Setting up a short daily riyaz routine and caring for the instrument and its strings between lessons

curriculum.title: Sargam, Alankar and a First Raag
topics: Playing ascending and descending sargam across the madhya and taar octaves in tune with the drone
Working through graded alankar and palta patterns to build strength and independence in the left hand
Repositioning the tied frets when a raag calls for komal or teevra swaras and then finding them accurately
Keeping the mizrab strokes even and unhurried while the left hand shifts position along the neck
Learning the aroha, avaroha and pakad of a first evening raag and recognising the mood it creates
Counting the sixteen matras of teentaal aloud and landing each phrase neatly on sam
Sounding the chikari strings between phrases to mark the shape of the rhythmic cycle
Playing a short fixed composition from memory over a tanpura or an electronic shruti drone

curriculum.title: Meend, Ornament and the Maseetkhani Gat
topics: Pulling the baj string sideways across the curved frets to produce a controlled meend of two or three swaras
Producing krintan and murki ornaments and grace-note kan swaras with the left hand alone, without a fresh mizrab stroke
Learning the slow Maseetkhani gat and the fixed pattern of da, ra and diri strokes that defines it
Playing the sthayi and antara sections of a slow gat and returning cleanly to sam each time
Adding simple todas that extend the gat while staying inside the grammar of the raag
Practising a morning raag alongside the evening raag already learnt and hearing how the two differ in mood
Tuning the tarab strings to the swaras of whichever raag is being practised before every session
Explaining the thaat, jaati, vadi and samvadi of every raag studied so far

curriculum.title: Razakhani Gat, Taan and Jhala
topics: Playing the fast Razakhani gat with a crisp and clearly articulated right hand
Building speed through taan patterns while keeping every swara distinctly separated
Playing jhala by alternating melody strokes on the baj string with rapid strumming of the chikari strings
Constructing tihais that resolve exactly on sam across three precise repetitions
Playing gats in jhaptaal and ektaal as fluently as in teentaal
Performing gats in three raags of contrasting times of day entirely from memory
Rehearsing with a tabla accompanist and holding a steady laya through gradual changes of tempo
Working towards the practical standard expected at intermediate Madhyama-level examinations

curriculum.title: Alaap, Jod and Raag Development
topics: Unfolding a raag in free rhythm through a slow alaap that reveals the swaras one at a time
Moving from alaap into jod, where a pulse emerges from the strokes themselves without any tabla to mark it
Developing a continuous alaap, jod and jhala sequence lasting around fifteen minutes
Improvising freely within the grammar of a raag rather than reciting fixed material
Using gamak, andolan and sustained meend to give the melodic line a vocal quality
Studying how phrasing, meend and stroke choice differ between the major sitar gharanas
Learning the ten-thaat classification, the twenty-two shrutis and how raags are grouped within them
Recording riyaz sessions and self-assessing intonation, stroke clarity and rhythmic accuracy

curriculum.title: Concert Craft and Recital
topics: Planning a full concert set that moves from alaap through a slow gat to a fast gat and jhala
Judging how far to develop each section for a given audience and a given time slot
Trading sawal-jawab phrases with a tabla player and closing each exchange together on sam
Tuning the sitar quickly and quietly on stage between items
Amplifying the sitar with a microphone or a pickup without losing its natural resonance
Performing three raags to recital standard with informed spoken introductions to each
Recording a practical portfolio of the standard expected at Visharad-level examinations
Designing a long-term riyaz schedule that sustains progress after the course finishes

name: Recorder
subtitle: Personalised live recorder coaching, from first notes on the descant to the Grade 5 standard.

curriculum.title: Level 1 – First Notes on the Descant Recorder
topics: Assembling the head, body and foot joints and lining the finger holes up in a straight row.
Holding the instrument with the left hand on top and the right hand below, with the thumbs supporting from behind.
Sealing each hole completely with the soft pad of the finger so that your first notes sound clear.
Blowing gently and steadily so that the note neither squeaks nor wavers.
Starting each note with a soft tongued syllable rather than a push of breath.
Playing three-note tunes first by ear and then from simple written notation.
Clapping and counting crotchet and minim rhythms before playing them on the instrument.
Swabbing the instrument dry and putting it away safely at the end of every session.

curriculum.title: Level 2 – Building the Range
topics: Adding the notes above the stave and the low notes that need every finger down.
Reading treble clef notation and naming the notes on the lines and in the spaces.
Playing one-octave scales and arpeggios in the easier sharp and flat keys.
Tonguing quaver passages evenly so that every note begins at exactly the right moment.
Taking a relaxed breath at a marked rest instead of breaking a phrase in half.
Playing simple duets with your teacher taking the second part underneath you.
Keeping a steady pulse against a metronome and resisting the urge to speed up in the easy bars.
Preparing three short contrasting pieces to the standard of a Grade 1 examination.

curriculum.title: Level 3 – Thumbing and the Upper Register
topics: Pinching the thumb hole slightly open to sound the notes of the second octave.
Controlling breath pressure so that the upper notes speak clearly instead of shrieking.
Learning the forked fingerings and using them fluently inside scale passages.
Playing scales and arpeggios in the wider set of keys expected at Grades 2 and 3.
Playing dotted rhythms and triplets accurately against a steady count.
Shaping dynamics through breath and articulation rather than raw volume, keeping the tuning stable as you do so.
Sight-reading a short unfamiliar melody, scanning it first for the awkward fingerings.
Performing a contrasting programme of pieces drawn from different musical periods.

curriculum.title: Level 4 – Articulation and the Treble Recorder
topics: Learning the treble recorder fingerings and transferring your reading onto an instrument pitched in F.
Using double tonguing to play fast repeated notes cleanly and evenly.
Adding trills and mordents with the correct auxiliary fingerings.
Playing chromatic passages that rely on half-holed fingerings.
Shaping baroque phrases with light articulation and gently tapered note endings.
Playing scales and arpeggios across the full two-octave range of the instrument.
Rehearsing with a keyboard or a recorded accompaniment and staying in tune with it.
Answering aural questions about pulse, dynamics and the shape of a phrase.

curriculum.title: Level 5 – Consort Playing and Grade 5 Standard
topics: Preparing a balanced three-piece programme at the Grade 5 standard on either descant or treble.
Playing extended fast passages with clean articulation and no loss of tone.
Warming the instrument before you play and pushing in or pulling out the head joint to bring it into tune.
Playing in a recorder consort and balancing your line against the parts above and below you.
Reading a short unfamiliar piece at sight, keeping going through slips rather than stopping to correct them.
Improvising simple divisions over a repeated bass line in the baroque manner.
Making a careful recording of two contrasting pieces to keep as a portfolio of your best playing.
Building a practice plan that shares your time between tone exercises, technical work and pieces.

name: Carnatic Violin
subtitle: Live one-to-one Carnatic violin lessons, from sarali varisai to kutcheri accompaniment.

curriculum.title: Sitting, Sruti and the First Swaras
topics: Sitting cross-legged on a mat with the back erect and the right foot drawn in so that it can carry the weight of the instrument.
Resting the scroll on the right ankle and letting the far end of the instrument settle against the left shoulder and collar bone.
Playing without a chin rest or a shoulder rest, so that the left hand stays free to slide the whole length of the string.
Retuning the strings away from the Western G, D, A and E to the Carnatic arrangement of Pa, Sa, Pa and Sa, moving the pegs first and settling the pitch with the fine tuners.
Fixing your own sruti against a tambura or sruti box, and learning that Sa and Pa have only one form while the other five swaras take several.
Drawing long, even bow strokes on each string in turn and holding a single swara steady against the drone.
Singing each swara aloud before you play it, so that the ear leads the fingers rather than the other way round.
Playing the seven swaras of Mayamalavagowla through one octave in the first speed, ascending and then descending.

curriculum.title: Varisai Foundations
topics: Working through the sarali varisai patterns in the first, second and third speeds without letting the pulse slip.
Keeping Adi tala with the right hand while you play, so that rhythm and melody stay linked from the very beginning.
Playing the janta varisai paired notes, re-articulating the repeated swara and giving the stress to the second of each pair.
Practising the dhatu varisai patterns, whose deliberate leaps train the fingers to move between distant swaras cleanly.
Extending your range upward with melsthayi varisai that add one higher swara at a time.
Reaching down into the lower octave with mandrasthayi varisai played on the two thicker strings.
Reading and writing swara notation, including the dots below and above a letter that mark the lower and higher octaves.
Getting every plain swara clear and in tune before any gamaka is attempted, so that ornament never disguises a poor note.

curriculum.title: Alankaram, Tala and the First Gamakas
topics: Playing the alankarams set to the sapta talas and showing each tala correctly with its beats, waves and finger counts.
Recognising the laghu, drutam and anudrutam and reproducing them with the hand while the bow keeps moving.
Treating gamaka as an oscillation and a slide between swaras, not as a Western vibrato added to a fixed note.
Producing the kampita gamaka by oscillating one finger along the string without lifting it, so that the pitch itself moves.
Playing geethams, the simple set compositions that join swara patterns to words and to a tala cycle.
Sliding a single finger along the string to reach the next swara, in place of the fixed finger positions Western playing relies on.
Distinguishing the varieties of Ri, Ga, Ma, Dha and Ni that give each raga its own individual character.
Playing against a recorded drone for several minutes at a stretch to build stamina and steady alignment with the sruti.

curriculum.title: Ragas, Varnam and Bowing Control
topics: Learning the arohanam and avarohanam of a set of common ragas and recognising each one by ear from a short phrase.
Playing the swarajathi, which links swara passages, tala and lyric within a single composition.
Working through an Adi tala varnam in two speeds, the milestone against which every Carnatic student is measured.
Matching the bow to the phrase so that a gamaka unfolds inside one continuous stroke instead of being chopped into separate notes.
Hiding the change of bow direction inside a sustained line so that the listener hears no break in the melody.
Transposing the janta and dhatu patterns into ragas other than Mayamalavagowla while keeping the correct swara varieties.
Understanding the melakarta system of parent scales and how the janya ragas are drawn from them.
Playing set pieces in three speeds against the tala until your rhythmic placement becomes automatic.

curriculum.title: Kritis and Manodharma
topics: Learning how the pallavi, anupallavi and charanam of a kriti are built and how each return of the theme is shaped.
Rendering sangatis, the progressively elaborated variations grown from a single pallavi line.
Improvising kalpanaswaram in phrases that land accurately on the eduppu, the point in the cycle where the line begins.
Beginning raga alapana by exploring a raga freely and without tala, phrase by unhurried phrase.
Playing neraval, expanding one line of text with fresh melodic and rhythmic ideas while its words stay in place.
Handling misra chapu, khanda chapu and rupaka talas alongside the familiar Adi tala.
Imitating the vocal idiom on the violin, since the Carnatic violin is expected to follow the singing voice closely.
Shadowing a vocalist's line in real time so that your sruti, phrasing and gamakas match theirs exactly.

curriculum.title: Kutcheri Practice and Accompaniment
topics: Taking the accompanist's role in a concert, following the main artist and answering in the gaps left for you.
Playing solo violin repertoire in which you carry both the composition and the improvisation yourself.
Building a concert-length list with a varnam to open, a substantial main item and lighter pieces to close.
Practising a ragam tanam pallavi in outline, setting a single pallavi line to a chosen tala and returning to it.
Keeping the tala through a mridangam player's tani avartanam and re-entering exactly on the eduppu.
Managing sruti, tuning and string care across the length of a full concert on stage.
Recording a complete recital and reviewing it for intonation, clarity of gamaka and the pacing of the programme.
Preparing an audition portfolio for sabha performances, competitions and music college entrance.

name: Carnatic Vocal Music
subtitle: Live one-to-one Carnatic vocal training, from varisai to kriti.

curriculum.title: Level 1: Sruti, Swara and Sarali Varisai
topics: Settling on a comfortable sruti and holding a steady adhara shadja against the tambura drone.
Singing the seven swaras in arohana and avarohana with clean pronunciation of every syllable.
Working through the sarali varisai in raga Mayamalavagowla, the scale traditionally given to beginners.
Keeping adi tala with the hand while singing, so the beats and the swaras stay locked together.
Learning simple akaara sadhakam on the open vowel to free the throat and lengthen every held note.
Building a daily sadhakam habit of twenty to thirty minutes that always begins with slow varisai.
Listening back to recordings of one's own practice to spot swaras that drift away from the sruti.

curriculum.title: Level 2: Janta, Dhaattu and Sthayi Varisai
topics: Singing janta varisai with paired swaras, giving each repeated note a clean, separated attack.
Extending the voice upward through mel sthayi varisai without straining or pushing the top notes.
Reaching down through mandra sthayi varisai to build a fuller, rounder tone in the lower octave.
Practising dhaattu varisai, where swaras leap out of sequence and test the singer's pitch memory.
Raising each exercise from the first kaalam to the second while the tala stays perfectly even.
Introducing basic gamaka, the oscillation that gives Carnatic swaras their characteristic shape.
Singing the sapta tala alankaram to feel all seven principal tala families in the body.

curriculum.title: Level 3: Geetham and Swarajathi
topics: Learning beginner geethams, which set simple devotional lyrics to one flowing line with no separate swara section.
Singing a geetham first in swaras and then in sahitya, so that words and notes are both secure.
Understanding how arohana and avarohana define the identity of every raga being sung.
Taking up swarajathi, in which passages of pure swara alternate with sections of sung sahitya.
Counting laghu, drutam and anudrutam correctly so the tala is shown as clearly as it is felt.
Pronouncing Sanskrit, Telugu, Tamil and Kannada syllables cleanly without breaking the melodic line.
Singing short compositions from memory rather than reading from written notation.

curriculum.title: Level 4: Varnam and Rhythmic Command
topics: Studying an adi tala varnam as the first piece that tests stamina, range and rhythm all at once.
Singing the pallavi, anupallavi, muktayi swaram and charanam with the phrasing each section needs.
Rendering the same varnam at both the first and the second kaalam within a single sitting.
Refining gamaka so a raga's characteristic bends sound built in rather than added on afterwards.
Managing breath across long phrases by deciding in advance exactly where to take air.
Giving the ettugada swaras that follow the charanam the weight and the finish they need.
Practising against a recorded mridangam or a metronome to hold tempo without the teacher present.

curriculum.title: Level 5: Kritis and Introduction to Manodharma
topics: Learning kritis of moderate difficulty and shaping the sangati variations that grow through them.
Opening a raga with a short alapana, exploring its swaras freely and outside any tala cycle.
Improvising kalpana swaram that lands accurately on the eduppu of the tala cycle.
Attempting neraval by resetting a single line of sahitya to fresh melodic ideas each time round.
Telling closely related ragas apart by their signature phrases rather than by their scale alone.
Bringing bhava, the emotional colour of the sahitya, into the singing instead of stating words plainly.
Building a small personal repertoire of pieces that can be sung reliably from memory.

curriculum.title: Level 6: Kutcheri Performance and Portfolio
topics: Planning a kutcheri in the traditional sequence, from a varnam opener through kritis to lighter closing pieces.
Rehearsing with violin and mridangam accompaniment, or with recorded tracks that stand in for them.
Balancing the tambura or sruti box against the voice on stage so the drone stays audible without swamping it.
Cueing the mridangist into the thani avartanam and picking the composition back up at the right point in the cycle.
Attempting a short ragam-tanam-pallavi as the centrepiece that draws every manodharma skill together.
Recovering smoothly when a swara or a line of sahitya slips during a live performance.
Preparing for an arangetram or a sabha appearance through full-length mock concerts under performance conditions.
Recording an audition portfolio of three contrasting items and reviewing each take to set the next term's sadhakam goals.

name: Hindustani Vocal Music
subtitle: Live one-to-one Hindustani vocal coaching, from kharaj to khayal.

curriculum.title: Level 1: Swar, Kharaj and a Steady Voice
topics: Finding a comfortable Sa against the tanpura and learning that Sa is a chosen pitch, never a fixed one.
Singing the seven shuddha swaras of the madhya saptak in aroh and avroh, the set that forms Bilawal thaat.
Practising kharaj sadhana in the mandra saptak to deepen and steady the natural tone.
Holding a single long note on aakar to test breath length and pitch stability honestly.
Learning the four komal swaras and tivra Madhyam, and hearing how each one changes the mood of a phrase.
Keeping teentaal with taali and khaali on the palm while singing until rhythm becomes automatic.
Setting up a daily riyaz routine that opens with kharaj and ends with a gentle cool-down.

curriculum.title: Level 2: Paltas, Alankar and Sargam Geet
topics: Working through graded paltas that carry one fixed pattern up and down the whole saptak.
Singing alankar first in vilambit and then in drut laya to build control and agility in turn.
Learning sargam geet, short compositions sung entirely in the names of the swaras.
Recognising the ten thaats of the Bhatkhande system and the family of raags that each one produces.
Identifying a raag from its aroh, avroh and pakad, the phrase that gives its identity away.
Practising dadra and kaherva alongside teentaal to feel six-, eight- and sixteen-beat cycles.
Singing light bhajans that use easy melodic movement and ask for clear, unhurried diction.

curriculum.title: Level 3: First Raags and Chhota Khayal
topics: Studying beginner raags such as Yaman, Bhairav and Bhoopali phrase by phrase rather than as bare scales.
Learning a chhota khayal bandish in drut laya and singing it against a live or recorded tabla.
Placing the sam accurately so that the mukhda of the bandish meets the first beat of the cycle.
Opening a raag with a short aalap that introduces its swaras one at a time, without tabla.
Adding meend, the smooth glide between swaras that binds a phrase into a single gesture.
Understanding the vadi and samvadi, the two swaras that a raag leans on most heavily.
Writing a bandish in Bhatkhande swaralipi so it can be revised without the teacher present.

curriculum.title: Level 4: Vistaar, Taan and Ornamentation
topics: Expanding a raag through vistaar, developing it phrase by phrase from the mandra saptak upward.
Practising sapaat taan, fast straight runs sung cleanly and evenly on a single breath.
Building alankarik and koot taan patterns that turn and twist within the swaras the raag allows.

name: Video Editing
subtitle: Personalised live video editing coaching, from first cut to finished showreel.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Footage, Story and the First Cut
topics: Understanding how a scene is built from wide, mid, close and cutaway shots working together
Importing rushes, organising them into bins and naming clips so that nothing goes missing later
Logging takes with in and out points and marking the genuinely usable part of every clip
Making a rough assembly on the timeline in story order before worrying about any polish
Closing gaps with ripple trims, then refining a join with roll, slip and slide edits that leave the running time untouched
Learning why a cut works by matching action, eye-line and screen direction across the join
Playing a first two-minute edit back to a listener and noting exactly where attention drifts

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Timeline Craft and Pacing
topics: Setting sequence resolution, frame rate and timecode so they match the original camera footage
Using three-point editing to drop a clip precisely into a marked gap in the timeline
Building J-cuts and L-cuts so that sound leads or trails the picture and the join disappears
Choosing between a straight cut, a dissolve and a wipe for a reason rather than out of habit
Cutting to the rhythm of music or dialogue and feeling how shot length controls the pace
Working with nested sequences and adjustment layers to keep a long edit manageable
Setting up proxy media so that heavy footage plays back smoothly on a modest laptop
Re-cutting the same footage two different ways to see how pacing changes the meaning

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Sound Design and the Mix
topics: Cleaning dialogue by removing hum, hiss and room noise without making the voice sound thin
Layering ambience, spot effects and foley so that a scene feels like a real place
Balancing dialogue, music and effects using faders and keyframed volume automation
Ducking music underneath speech so that the words always stay in front of everything else
Applying compression and equalisation lightly to give a voice presence and consistency
Metering the finished mix against the loudness target in LUFS that the destination platform expects
Syncing separately recorded audio to camera footage and correcting drift over a long take
Finishing a short scene in which the sound alone carries half of the storytelling

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Colour Correction and Grading
topics: Reading waveform, parade and vectorscope displays instead of trusting an uncalibrated screen
Correcting exposure and white balance shot by shot so a sequence matches from end to end
Shaping contrast deliberately with lift, gamma and gain controls and with curves
Working with log footage and understanding what a conversion look-up table actually does to it
Applying secondary corrections with masks, tracking and qualifiers to isolate skin tones or sky
Building one consistent look across a whole film and checking that it survives on a phone screen
Grading the same clip warm and then cool to see how colour alone changes the mood of a scene

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Titles, Motion Graphics and Finishing Effects
topics: Designing readable lower thirds and end credits that suit the film rather than fight it
Animating text and shapes with keyframes and easing so that movement feels intentional
Stabilising shaky handheld footage inside the edit and recognising when a shot simply cannot be saved
Masking and tracking a quick fix through a shot, such as blurring a number plate as it moves
Speed-ramping a clip and using time remapping for slow motion and sudden speed changes
Adding subtitles and burnt-in captions, including in Indian language scripts
Reframing a horizontal edit for vertical delivery without destroying the original composition

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Delivery, Client Work and Showreel
topics: Choosing a codec, bitrate and container suited to the destination, whether social, broadcast or archive
Exporting a high-quality master file and generating lighter versions for review and for upload
Managing an archive of projects, media and backups so an old edit can be reopened years later
Running a client review round, collecting timecoded notes and turning them into a clear change list
Working to a brief and a fixed deadline on a real short commission from start through to delivery
Quoting a small editing job in rupees and agreeing in advance how many revision rounds are included
Cutting a sixty-second showreel that opens with the single strongest piece of work
Presenting the finished reel and two complete films in a live portfolio review

short_description: Personalised live video editing coaching, from first cut to finished showreel.

name: Animation
subtitle: Personalised live animation coaching, from bouncing ball to finished short film.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Movement, Timing and the Bouncing Ball
topics: Discovering how a sequence of still drawings becomes movement and what frames per second really means
Flipping a hand-made paper flipbook to feel the connection between spacing and apparent speed
Animating a bouncing ball and adjusting the timing chart until it feels heavy or light
Applying squash and stretch to the ball while keeping its volume convincingly constant
Learning slow in and slow out so that movement accelerates and then settles naturally
Tracing arcs across the frame so that nothing ever travels in a dead straight line
Setting up onion skinning and a simple exposure sheet inside a drawing programme
Finishing a five-second animation of a ball travelling through a small obstacle course

curriculum.title: Level 2 — The Principles in Practice
topics: Building anticipation into an action so the audience reads it just before it happens
Adding follow-through and overlapping action to hair, cloth and trailing limbs
Comparing the straight-ahead and pose-to-pose working methods on the very same shot
Using exaggeration to push a pose past the literal so that the idea reads instantly
Staging a shot so that the silhouette alone tells the viewer what is happening
Adding a secondary action that supports the main movement instead of competing with it
Animating a simple flour-sack character that shows weight, effort and emotion without a face

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Character, Drawing and Walk Cycles
topics: Designing a character from simple shapes and keeping it on model from every angle
Building a turnaround and an expression sheet to act as reference for the whole production
Constructing a walk cycle with the contact, down, passing and up positions
Adapting that cycle into a run, a sneak and a tired trudge to reveal personality
Animating a head turn along an arc with correct overlap between eyes, head and hair
Working on ones and on twos and knowing which choice suits a particular shot
Drawing hands and simple gestures that still read clearly at a small screen size

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Digital Rigs and Keyframe Animation
topics: Cutting a character into layers and joining them into a sensible parented hierarchy
Rigging bones with inverse kinematics so that an arm or a leg moves as a connected chain
Setting keyframes on position, rotation and scale and then refining the interpolation between them
Reading and editing the graph editor so that eases and holds behave exactly as intended
Building a mouth chart of visemes and swapping the shapes to lip-sync a short recorded line
Animating a cut-out puppet through a full action while keeping the drawing consistent
Rigging a simple prop that the character can pick up, carry and hand over
Cleaning up a scene file so that another animator could take it over without confusion

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Story, Storyboard and Animatic
topics: Writing a one-page story idea with a clear beginning, a turn and a satisfying ending
Thumbnailing shots and choosing camera angles that serve the emotion of each story beat
Drawing a storyboard with arrows and notes that another person could animate directly from
Cutting the boards into a timed animatic with scratch dialogue and temporary sound
Judging pacing from the animatic and cutting weak shots before any animation is made
Designing backgrounds and a colour script that carry the mood through the whole film
Planning a realistic production schedule so that a short film actually reaches completion

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Producing a Finished Short
topics: Animating the key poses across every shot and reviewing the whole film in rough form
Adding inbetweens and clean-up so that the linework stays consistent from shot to shot
Colouring and shading scenes with a set palette and a light source that makes physical sense
Compositing characters over backgrounds with camera moves, depth and simple atmospheric effects
Recording and editing dialogue, music and sound effects precisely to picture
Rendering the film at the correct resolution and frame rate for screening and for the web
Screening the finished short to an audience and taking honest notes from their reaction
Cutting a reel of the strongest character performances, each shown from rough pose test through to final colour

short_description: Personalised live animation coaching, from bouncing ball to finished short film.

name: VFX
subtitle: Personalised live VFX coaching, from green screen to finished breakdown reel.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — How a Visual Effect Is Built
topics: Breaking an effects shot into plate, elements and matte to see how the illusion is assembled
Understanding alpha channels and premultiplication and what transparency actually stores
Learning the practical difference between a layer-based and a node-based compositing workflow
Reading a node graph and following the path a single pixel takes from input to final output
Working in a linear colour space and understanding why a composite goes wrong in the wrong one
Managing image sequences, frame ranges and high dynamic range file formats such as EXR
Rebuilding a simple two-layer composite from supplied plates and matching the reference

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Keying and Matte Extraction
topics: Assessing a green-screen plate for spill, uneven lighting and motion blur before starting the key
Pulling a core key with a chroma keyer and refining the edges without eating away fine hair
Combining a core matte, an edge matte and a holdout matte into one clean composite matte
Removing green spill from the subject and replacing it with light from the new background
Using luminance keys and difference keys in situations where a chroma key will not work
Adding edge blend, light wrap and matched defocus so the cutout stops looking pasted on
Advising a crew on how to light and shoot a green screen so the key is far easier afterwards

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Rotoscoping and Paint
topics: Drawing roto shapes that follow the form of a limb rather than tracing a random outline
Keyframing shapes on key positions and letting the software interpolate the frames between
Adding motion blur to a roto matte so that it matches the speed of the underlying plate
Splitting a figure into separate shapes for each body part to get cleaner articulation
Using planar tracking to drive shapes across a surface with far fewer manual keyframes
Painting out rigs, wires, tracking markers and unwanted objects with clone and patch techniques
Rebuilding a clean plate that can then be reused across an entire shot

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Tracking and Match-Move
topics: Choosing high-contrast features that survive across the whole shot for reliable point tracking
Stabilising a plate, working on it, and then reapplying the original camera movement afterwards
Corner-pinning a screen replacement onto a moving phone, monitor or roadside hoarding
Solving a 3D camera from a moving shot and checking that solve back against the plate
Undistorting a plate before the solve and redistorting the render again at the very end
Setting world scale and the ground plane so that inserted objects sit at a believable size
Testing a solve with tracking geometry and diagnosing the causes of a track that slips

curriculum.title: Level 5 — CG Integration and Effects Elements
topics: Merging rendered CG over a plate using render passes such as diffuse, specular and depth
Matching the direction, colour and softness of the plate lighting onto the CG element
Building contact shadows, reflections and interaction so the element belongs in the scene
Simulating sparks, rain and dust with a particle system and smoke with a simple fluid solve
Adding atmospheric depth using fog, haze and depth-based defocus across the frame
Matching lens character with distortion, chromatic aberration, bloom and film grain
Comparing the composite against real reference footage and fixing whatever gives it away
Reviewing the shot on a large screen where every remaining mistake becomes obvious

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Shot Delivery and Breakdown Reel
topics: Planning an effects shot from the client brief through to a written methodology
Building a template setup so that several shots in one sequence share the same structure
Working through a supervisor's notes across review rounds and versioning every submission
Optimising a heavy composite with pre-renders and proxies so that it stays workable
Rendering final frames with the correct colour transform and delivery specification
Cutting a breakdown that reveals each layer of a shot from raw plate through to final
Assembling a demo reel with a written shot list stating exactly which task was personally done
Preparing for a studio interview by explaining the technical choices in a shot out loud

short_description: Personalised live VFX coaching, from green screen to finished breakdown reel.

name: AWS
subtitle: Live AWS coaching from cloud fundamentals to EC2, S3 and IAM, finishing with Cloud Practitioner exam readiness.

curriculum.title: Cloud Computing Foundations
topics: Understanding what cloud computing is by comparing rented on-demand capacity with buying and housing servers outright.
Distinguishing infrastructure, platform and software service models and recognising who manages what in each one.
Learning why elasticity, agility and pay-as-you-go economics changed the way organisations build systems.
Mapping regions, availability zones and edge locations, then choosing a sensible region for an Indian user base.
Navigating the management console and seeing how the command line interface and the software development kits reach the same services.
Reading the shared responsibility model to separate the security duties of the provider from those of the customer.
Creating a personal free-tier account safely and switching on a billing alert before launching anything at all.
Comparing cloud, hybrid and on-premises deployment approaches against realistic business examples.

curriculum.title: Compute Services and EC2
topics: Launching a first virtual server and choosing its machine image, instance type and attached storage.
Understanding instance families and picking a general purpose, compute optimised or memory optimised type for a workload.
Creating and protecting a key pair, then connecting to a running instance over a secure shell session.
Configuring security groups so only the ports an application genuinely needs are ever reachable.
Comparing on-demand, reserved, savings plan and spot purchase options and working out which suits a steady workload.
Attaching elastic block store volumes, taking snapshots and restoring a volume from an earlier snapshot.
Placing an auto scaling group behind a load balancer so capacity is added when traffic rises and removed when it falls.
Recognising when a serverless function or a managed container service fits a workload better than a full virtual server.

curriculum.title: Storage and Databases
topics: Explaining the difference between object, block and file storage and choosing correctly for a given kind of data.
Creating an object storage bucket, uploading files and understanding how object keys and prefixes organise the data.
Applying storage classes and lifecycle rules so rarely used data moves automatically to cheaper tiers.
Configuring versioning and server-side encryption to protect stored objects from accidental deletion and exposure.
Hosting a static website from a bucket and serving it faster to distant users through a content delivery network.
Launching a managed relational database and working with its automated backups, snapshots and read replicas.
Comparing a managed relational service with a managed key-value service and matching each to a real application pattern.
Estimating monthly storage and data transfer charges for a small project and reading the figure in rupee terms.

curriculum.title: Identity, Security and Networking
topics: Understanding why the root user should be locked away and used only for the handful of tasks that require it.
Creating users, groups and roles and applying the principle of least privilege to every one of them.
Reading and writing a simple identity policy document to see exactly which actions it allows or denies.
Enabling multi-factor authentication and explaining how it stops a stolen password from being useful on its own.
Designing a virtual private cloud with public and private subnets, route tables and an internet gateway.
Contrasting security groups with network access control lists and knowing that the group is stateful while the list is not.
Using the managed key, certificate and secret storage services to keep credentials out of application code.
Reviewing compliance report downloads, audit logging and managed denial-of-service protection to the depth a practitioner needs.

curriculum.title: Monitoring, Cost Control and Support
topics: Collecting metrics, publishing logs and setting alarms so a team is warned about trouble before its users notice.
Tracking who did what, when and from where through account activity and audit trail logging.
Using the pricing calculator to estimate the monthly cost of a small three-tier application before it is built.
Reading the billing dashboard, applying cost allocation tags and setting budget alerts in rupee terms.
Comparing the published support plans and knowing which tiers include a technical account manager and faster response targets.
Running the automated account checks that flag unused resources, open security gaps and available savings.
Understanding consolidated billing and organisation-level guardrails across several linked accounts.
Applying the well-architected pillars as a practical checklist when reviewing any design.

curriculum.title: Capstone Project and Practitioner Readiness
topics: Designing a complete small architecture for a realistic Indian business scenario such as an online store.
Building that design hands-on with compute, storage, database and networking services working together.
Securing the build with roles, encryption and least-privilege access rather than convenient open permissions.
Documenting the architecture with a clear diagram and a written justification for every service chosen.
Revising the four Cloud Practitioner domains of cloud concepts, security and compliance, cloud technology and services, and billing, pricing and support.
Practising timed multiple-choice and multiple-response questions in the exam style and analysing every wrong answer.
Learning the exam-day mechanics, including question format, scoring, timing and how a test slot is booked.
Tearing down every project resource cleanly so no unexpected charges continue after the course ends.

short_description: Live AWS coaching from cloud fundamentals to EC2, S3 and IAM, finishing with Cloud Practitioner exam readiness.

name: DevOps
subtitle: Live DevOps mentoring across Linux, Git, continuous delivery pipelines, Docker, Kubernetes and monitoring.

curriculum.title: DevOps Foundations and the Linux Command Line
topics: Understanding why development and operations teams merged and what problems the old hand-over model caused.
Distinguishing continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment, and seeing how each builds on the one before it.
Navigating a Linux filesystem confidently with commands for moving, copying, searching and inspecting files.
Managing permissions, users and running processes on a server without any graphical interface at all.
Writing a shell script that automates a repetitive task such as archiving log files every night.
Installing packages, managing services and reading system logs to diagnose a failing application.
Connecting to a remote server over secure shell using key-based authentication instead of passwords.
Measuring delivery health through lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore service.

curriculum.title: Version Control with Git
topics: Initialising a repository and recording changes as commits with clear and genuinely useful messages.
Understanding the working directory, the staging area and the repository as three distinct places a change can sit.
Creating branches to develop features in isolation and merging them back once they are ready.
Resolving a merge conflict by reading both sides of the change and deciding what the final file should say.
Working with remote repositories through cloning, fetching, pulling and pushing.
Raising a pull request, reviewing a teammate's code and responding to review comments constructively.
Comparing trunk-based development with longer-lived branching strategies and their release implications.
Recovering from mistakes using revert, reset and the reference log without losing the team's work.

curriculum.title: Build Automation and Continuous Integration
topics: Setting up a pipeline that builds and tests an application automatically on every push.
Writing the pipeline configuration as a file kept in the repository alongside the application code.
Running unit tests, linting and code quality checks as gates that block a broken build from progressing.
Managing build artefacts and dependency caching so pipelines finish in minutes rather than hours.
Storing secrets and credentials in the pipeline's own secure store instead of hard-coding them into scripts.
Triggering different pipeline behaviour for feature branches, the main branch and tagged releases.
Reading a failed pipeline log and tracing the failure back to the exact commit that caused it.
Adding build status notifications so the whole team learns about a red build immediately.

curriculum.title: Containers with Docker
topics: Explaining how containers share the host kernel while virtual machines do not, and why that makes them start in seconds.
Writing a Dockerfile that installs dependencies and packages an application into a reproducible image.
Building, tagging and pushing images to a registry, then pulling them down onto a different machine.
Running containers with port mapping, environment variables and sensible memory and processor limits.
Persisting data with volumes so information survives when a container is replaced.
Connecting several containers on a shared network so an application and its database can talk to each other.
Defining a multi-container local environment in a compose file so the whole stack starts with one command.
Reducing image size with multi-stage builds and scanning finished images for known vulnerabilities.

curriculum.title: Orchestration and Infrastructure as Code
topics: Understanding why a scheduler becomes necessary once an application runs as many containers across many machines.
Deploying a first workload as pods managed by a deployment and exposing it through a service.
Scaling a deployment up and down and performing a rolling update without taking the service offline.
Supplying configuration values and secrets to workloads without rebuilding the container image.
Reading pod logs and inspecting resources to diagnose a workload stuck in a crash loop.
Declaring cloud infrastructure in code so an entire environment can be recreated identically on demand.
Running a plan before every apply so each infrastructure change is reviewed before it actually happens.
Managing state files and reusable modules so infrastructure code stays safe and tidy across a team.

curriculum.title: Monitoring, Reliability and Capstone Pipeline
topics: Collecting metrics from applications and servers and visualising them on a dashboard the whole team reads.
Aggregating logs centrally so a single error can be traced across several services at once.
Adding distributed tracing to follow one user request through a long chain of services.
Defining alerts tied to real user impact rather than firing on every small fluctuation.
Setting service level objectives and using an error budget to balance new features against stability.
Running a blameless incident review that produces concrete engineering fixes rather than assigning fault.
Building an end-to-end capstone that carries a commit through build, test, image, deployment and monitoring automatically.
Presenting that capstone pipeline with a written runbook covering rollback and on-call handover.

short_description: Live DevOps mentoring across Linux, Git, continuous delivery pipelines, Docker, Kubernetes and monitoring.

name: Rubik's Cube
subtitle: Live cube coaching, from your very first complete solve to sub-twenty-second speedcubing.

curriculum.title: Notation, the Cross and the First Layer
topics: Naming the six faces of the cube and learning the single letters used to write down every possible turn.
Reading clockwise, anticlockwise and double turns from written notation so that any algorithm can be followed exactly.
Understanding that the six centre pieces never change places relative to one another, so each centre fixes the colour of its face.
Telling edges apart from corners by counting their stickers, and seeing that no piece can ever change from one type into the other.
Building the white cross so that each edge matches both the white centre and the side centre standing next to it.
Inserting the four white corners one at a time to finish the first layer without breaking the cross underneath.
Turning the cube in your hands and re-gripping smoothly instead of putting it down between every step.
Practising the first layer daily until it can be solved from any scramble without a single prompt from the coach.

curriculum.title: Completing the Cube: Layer by Layer
topics: Placing the four middle-layer edges using the right-hand and left-hand insertion sequences.
Forming the yellow cross on the top face from the dot, the line and the L-shaped starting cases.
Aligning the top edges with their matching centres before any attention is given to the corners.
Positioning the last-layer corners into their correct places even while they are still twisted the wrong way.
Twisting the final corners with the repeated sequence while holding the cube in one fixed orientation throughout.
Recovering calmly when a sequence is mis-applied and the cube suddenly looks scrambled all over again.
Completing a full unaided solve from a scramble and timing it honestly with a stopwatch.
Explaining the whole method aloud to a friend or parent to prove that it is genuinely understood.

curriculum.title: Faster Beginner Solves and an Efficient Cross
topics: Solving the cross on the bottom of the cube so that the layer you build next stays in full view.
Planning the entire cross during the fifteen seconds of inspection that official competition allows.
Cutting the cross down to eight moves or fewer by choosing an efficient order and solving edges together rather than one after another.
Learning basic finger tricks so that the fingers and thumbs do the turning instead of the whole wrist.
Adjusting the tension and lubrication of your own cube so that the turns stay quick without the pieces popping out.
Removing pauses from the solve by counting the moves spent on each individual stage.
Keeping a simple log of your times so that the weekly average can be watched falling.
Bringing a complete solve comfortably under one minute as a settled average rather than as a lucky one-off.

curriculum.title: CFOP Stage One: Intuitive First Two Layers
topics: Understanding why pairing a corner with its matching edge beats solving the two pieces one after the other.
Building corner and edge pairs intuitively instead of trying to memorise all forty-one cases at once.
Handling the straightforward cases in which the pair is already formed and needs only to be inserted.
Separating a pair that is trapped in the wrong slot before rebuilding it in the slot where it belongs.
Using all four slots and rotating the whole cube as little as possible during the solve.
Practising lookahead by tracking the next pair while the current one is still being inserted.
Turning deliberately slowly in training so that hand speed never outruns your recognition.
Finishing the first two layers in one flowing sequence with no long hesitations anywhere in it.

curriculum.title: CFOP Stage Two: Orienting and Permuting the Last Layer
topics: Splitting the last layer into two separate jobs, first turning every yellow sticker upwards and then moving the pieces into their places.
Learning two-look orientation with three edge cases followed by seven corner cases.
Learning two-look permutation with a compact set of corner and edge sequences.
Recognising each case instantly from its sticker pattern rather than working it out from scratch every time.
Expanding gradually towards the full set of fifty-seven orientation algorithms.
Adding the twenty-one permutation algorithms and drilling hardest on the ones that appear most often.
Choosing the best holding angle so that recognition happens before the turning has to begin.
Driving the average solve time steadily downwards towards twenty seconds.

curriculum.title: Speedcubing Practice and Competition
topics: Training with official-style scrambles and a proper timer using the competition start and stop procedure.
Following the fifteen-second inspection rule and knowing that a small overrun costs two seconds while a larger one costs the whole solve.
Recording an average of five and an average of twelve the official way, with the fastest and slowest solves dropped.
Replaying a slow solve move by move to identify the stage that is costing you the most time.
Understanding how a World Cube Association round is run, from the judge and the scorecard to the cut-off for the round.
Working through the registration procedure for a competition held in India and reading the day's schedule before you travel.
Applying the reduction method on the 4x4 so that it finishes as an ordinary 3x3 solve, and learning the different approaches that the 2x2 and the Pyraminx need.
Performing a confident solve in front of an audience and then guiding a beginner through their own first complete solve.

short_description: Live cube coaching, from your very first complete solve to sub-twenty-second speedcubing.

name: Chess
subtitle: Live one-to-one chess coaching, from the first moves on the board to rated tournament play.

curriculum.title: Board, Pieces and First Moves
topics: Setting the board up correctly every single time, with a light square in the right-hand corner and each queen standing on her own colour.
Learning how the rook, bishop, queen and king move and capture before tackling the awkward L-shaped jump of the knight.
Understanding that a pawn steps straight forward but captures diagonally, and may move two squares only from its starting rank.
Comparing the rough value of the pieces so that a rook counted as five is understood to be worth more than a bishop or a knight counted as three.
Practising the three special moves of castling, pawn promotion and capturing en passant until each of them feels ordinary.
Recognising check, checkmate and stalemate, and explaining in your own words why a stalemate only ever counts as a draw.
Delivering the basic checkmate with king and queen against a lone king without stumbling into stalemate at the last moment.
Playing full slow games against the coach, writing each move down in algebraic notation and touching only the piece you intend to move.

curriculum.title: Opening Principles and Basic Tactics
topics: Fighting for the four central squares with pawns and pieces from the very first move of the game.
Developing the knights and bishops quickly instead of moving the same piece twice while the rest of the army sleeps.
Castling early to tuck the king into safety and to connect the rooks along the back rank.
Spotting forks, where a single knight or pawn attacks two enemy pieces at exactly the same moment.
Setting up pins that freeze a defender, and telling an absolute pin against the king apart from a relative one.
Winning material with skewers by attacking a big piece first and collecting the smaller one standing behind it.
Uncovering discovered attacks and discovered checks by stepping one piece out of the line of another.
Solving a timed puzzle set each week and explaining the winning idea aloud before any piece is touched.

curriculum.title: Checkmating Patterns and Basic Endgames
topics: Driving a lone king to the edge of the board and mating first with two rooks and then with a single rook and king.
Learning the back-rank mate and the quiet pawn move that gives your own king an escape square before the danger arrives.
Practising the smothered mate, the Arabian mate and the other repeating checkmating shapes that appear again and again.
Using the opposition in king and pawn endings to shoulder the enemy king out of the way of your pawn.
Working out the square of the pawn in order to judge whether a king can catch a running passed pawn.
Escorting a passed pawn to promotion with the king marching in front of it rather than trailing behind.
Understanding why a single extra pawn matters far more once the queens have left the board.
Converting winning endings against the coach from set positions with a clock ticking beside you.

curriculum.title: Middlegame Plans and Attacking Play
topics: Making a simple plan by asking which side of the board your own pawn chain is pointing towards.
Doubling the rooks on an open file and invading the seventh rank, where they attack pawns that cannot run away.
Finding outpost squares for a knight where no enemy pawn can ever chase it away again.
Attacking a castled king with a pawn storm while keeping your own king safely out of the counter-attack.
Judging when the bishop sacrifice on h7 or f7 is genuinely sound and when it simply throws a piece away.
Combining two tactics in sequence, such as a deflection that clears the way for a fork on the following move.
Defending accurately by naming the opponent's threat out loud before choosing any move of your own.
Analysing your own lost games to pinpoint the exact move at which the position turned against you.

curriculum.title: Opening Repertoire and Rated Tournament Play
topics: Building a small and reliable repertoire of one opening for White and two defences for Black.
Understanding the typical middlegame plans that grow out of your chosen openings instead of memorising long forced lines.
Managing the clock in rapid and classical time controls so that a winning position is never lost on time.
Following tournament etiquette, scoresheet rules and the touch-move law as an arbiter applies them.
Understanding how the FIDE Elo system and the national rating ladder of the All India Chess Federation are calculated.
Planning a season of rated events with your parents and budgeting the entry fees and travel costs in rupees.
Coping when an opponent leaves your preparation on move four by falling back on general principles rather than panicking.
Building a personal database of your own games and tagging every mistake by the theme that caused it.

curriculum.title: Competitive Performance and Rating Growth
topics: Playing full-length practice games under strict tournament conditions with a clock, a scoresheet and no interruptions.
Reviewing each game with the coach unaided first, and only then checking the critical moments with an engine.
Keeping a personal opening file that is corrected and extended after every event you play.
Handling nerves, long playing sessions and a painful loss without carrying any of it into the following round.
Setting a realistic rating target and tracking your progress across both the national and the FIDE rating lists.
Agreeing a short pre-game routine with the coach so that every round begins in the same settled frame of mind.
Guiding a younger player through a simple position, which sharpens your own understanding as much as theirs.
Completing a simulated tournament of graded games followed by a written report on your performance.

short_description: Live one-to-one chess coaching, from the first moves on the board to rated tournament play.

name: Arts & Painting
subtitle: Live drawing and painting coaching, from the first pencil marks to a finished portfolio.

curriculum.title: Level 1: Drawing Foundations
topics: Holding the pencil in both an overhand and a writing grip to control light and heavy marks.
Drawing straight lines, ellipses and even curves freehand without reaching for a ruler.
Breaking everyday objects down into the underlying cube, sphere, cone and cylinder.
Measuring proportion by sighting along a pencil held at arm's length with the elbow locked.
Practising blind contour drawing by following an object's edge without looking at the paper.
Comparing graphite grades from 2H through HB to 6B and choosing the right pencil for each mark.
Keeping a daily sketchbook of small observational studies drawn from life at home.

curriculum.title: Level 2: Light, Shade and Form
topics: Building a value scale of at least seven even steps from white to the darkest graphite black.
Shading with hatching, cross-hatching, stippling and smooth continuous blending.
Finding the light source, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow on a single sphere.
Drawing a still life of three objects lit by one strong lamp placed to the side.
Rendering the difference between cloth, polished metal, glass and the skin of a fruit.
Lifting highlights out with a kneaded eraser rather than using it only to correct mistakes.
Checking that the drawing still reads clearly when squinted at or seen from across the room.

curriculum.title: Level 3: Perspective and Composition
topics: Setting a horizon line and a single vanishing point to draw a road or a corridor receding.
Constructing boxes and buildings in two-point perspective from a chosen eye level.
Dividing the rectangle by thirds and by diagonals to decide where the focal point sits.
Using overlap, diminishing size and atmospheric haze to push objects into the distance.
Drawing a room interior with furniture that sits convincingly on the floor plane.
Testing three small thumbnail layouts before committing to the full-size drawing.
Leading the viewer's eye with directional lines, tonal contrast and repeated shapes.

curriculum.title: Level 4: Colour and Watercolour
topics: Mixing a full colour wheel from the three primaries alone and recording every mix for reference.
Separating hue, value and saturation so that each can be adjusted without disturbing the others.
Choosing complementary, analogous and deliberately limited palettes to set the mood of a picture.
Stretching and taping watercolour paper so the sheet stays flat when it is heavily wetted.
Laying flat, graded and variegated washes with a large, well-loaded round or mop brush.
Painting wet-on-wet for soft skies and wet-on-dry for crisp, controlled edges.
Reserving the white of the paper for highlights instead of adding opaque white afterwards.
Neutralising a colour with its complement to mix convincing greys and browns.

curriculum.title: Level 5: Acrylic and Painting Technique
topics: Priming canvas or board with gesso and laying a toned ground before drawing the subject in.
Working from a thin underpainting towards thicker, more opaque layers as the picture develops.
Producing different textures with a loaded flat brush and with the edge of a palette knife.
Glazing a transparent layer over dry paint to deepen colour without burying the detail beneath.
Keeping acrylics workable with a stay-wet palette and an occasional light mist of water.
Painting a landscape in clearly separated bands of foreground, middle ground and distance.
Completing an alla prima study of one object in a single sitting while the paint stays open.
Washing and reshaping brushes straight after use so a starter set lasts several terms.

curriculum.title: Level 6: Portfolio and Personal Style
topics: Choosing a subject strong enough to carry four to six related finished works.
Studying two artists whose handling of colour or mark-making suits the chosen theme.
Carrying one idea from thumbnails through colour studies to a full-scale final painting.
Deciding the best medium for each piece and staying with that decision through to the end.
Critiquing your own week's work against value, colour, edges and composition in turn.
Photographing paintings square-on in even light and correcting the crop afterwards.
Sequencing a portfolio so that it opens and closes with the strongest images.
Writing a short artist's statement that explains the theme and the methods behind it.

short_description: Live drawing and painting coaching, from the first pencil marks to a finished portfolio.
description:
Why Choose Online Arts and Painting Classes?

In a world where screens dominate our daily lives, it's no surprise that the realm of education has also shifted its focus to the digital sphere. Online learning platforms have revolutionized how we acquire new skills, and the realm of arts and painting is no exception. Whether you're a seasoned artist or an eager beginner, the benefits of enrolling in online arts and painting classes are boundless. Here's why you should consider embracing the virtual canvas:

name: Creative Writing
subtitle: Live coaching that carries a young writer from a first idea to a finished, edited story.

curriculum.title: Level 1: Finding Ideas and Getting Started
topics: Keeping an ideas notebook of overheard lines, odd sights and unusual names.
Freewriting for ten minutes without stopping in order to quieten the inner critic.
Turning a single photograph or object into three completely different story openings.
Describing a familiar place through sound, smell and touch as well as through sight.
Replacing vague words with precise nouns and strong verbs that do the work of adjectives.
Reading your own paragraph aloud to hear exactly where the sentence stumbles.
Setting a realistic weekly writing habit and keeping to it between classes.

curriculum.title: Level 2: Character and Voice
topics: Building a character profile covering what they want, what they fear and one contradiction.
Revealing personality through action and choice instead of through a list of adjectives.
Writing the same short scene twice from two different characters' points of view.
Choosing between first and third person and testing which one suits the story better.
Giving each character a distinct rhythm of speech and one telling physical habit.
Creating an obstacle that forces the main character to change by the last page.
Sketching a minor character who does one memorable thing and then leaves the story.

curriculum.title: Level 3: Setting, Atmosphere and World
topics: Grounding a scene with three concrete details rather than a long block of description.
Using weather, sound and light to set the mood without ever naming the emotion.
Writing an Indian street, kitchen or classroom so vividly that a stranger can picture it.
Deciding the rules of an invented world and keeping them consistent all the way through.
Cutting description that stops the story from moving forward.
Letting the place on the page reflect what the main character is feeling in that moment.
Researching a real setting without dropping raw facts into the middle of the prose.

curriculum.title: Level 4: Plot, Structure and Tension
topics: Shaping a story arc of setup, rising trouble, climax and resolution.
Raising the stakes so that each scene costs the character more than the one before it.
Planting an early detail that pays off in the closing scene.
Entering a scene late and leaving it early so the pace stays tight.
Writing a chapter ending that makes the reader turn the page immediately.
Choosing between a happy, a bittersweet and an open ending, and justifying that choice.
Outlining a whole story on index cards before writing the first draft.
Diagnosing a sagging middle and repairing it with a fresh complication.

curriculum.title: Level 5: Dialogue, Style and Craft
topics: Punctuating speech correctly and varying where the speech tag falls in the line.
Writing dialogue that carries conflict instead of politely swapping information.
Using subtext so that a character says one thing and clearly means another.
Balancing dialogue, action beats and silence within a single scene.
Varying sentence length deliberately to speed a passage up or slow it down.
Inventing fresh comparisons and retiring similes that have been worn smooth by use.
Stretching range by attempting a poem, a monologue and a piece of flash fiction.

curriculum.title: Level 6: Editing and the Finished Piece
topics: Letting a finished draft rest for several days before rereading it with fresh eyes.
Revising for structure first, then for language, and only last for spelling and punctuation.
Cutting a tenth of the word count without losing any of the meaning.
Giving and receiving workshop feedback that is specific enough to be acted on.
Formatting a manuscript neatly with a title page, clean spacing and numbered pages.
Preparing a piece for a school magazine or for a children's writing competition.
Choosing a title and a closing line strong enough to stand for the whole story.
Planning the next project out of what this finished piece has taught you.

short_description: Live coaching that carries a young writer from a first idea to a finished, edited story.

name: Public Speaking
subtitle: Live coaching in confidence, voice and stagecraft for young speakers.

curriculum.title: Level 1: Confidence and First Words
topics: Introducing yourself for one minute using a simple three-part opening.
Standing with the feet planted, the shoulders open and the hands out of your pockets.
Holding steady eye contact with different parts of the room, or with the camera lens online.
Replacing filler sounds such as um and like with a short deliberate silence.
Warming up with breathing, humming and tongue twisters before every session.
Speaking about a favourite object for two minutes in a show-and-tell round.
Recognising nerves as ordinary body signals and settling them with slow breathing.

curriculum.title: Level 2: Voice, Breath and Delivery
topics: Breathing low from the diaphragm so that the last word of a sentence still carries.
Projecting to the back of a hall without shouting or straining the throat.
Varying pitch, pace and volume so that the audience keeps listening.
Pausing deliberately just before and just after an important idea.
Articulating consonant endings clearly so that words do not run into each other.
Marking a script with stress and pause symbols before rehearsing it aloud.
Recording yourself, listening back and naming one specific thing to change next time.
Looking after the voice with water, rest and no habitual throat clearing.

curriculum.title: Level 3: Building a Speech
topics: Narrowing a broad topic into one sentence that states your main message.
Opening with a question, a striking figure or a short scene that earns attention.
Organising the body into three points, each with an example and a linking line.
Closing with a call to action that echoes the words of the opening.
Checking a claim against a reliable source and crediting that source aloud in one phrase.
Timing a draft and trimming it to fit a three-minute or a five-minute slot.
Speaking from cue cards that carry keywords rather than a fully written script.

curriculum.title: Level 4: Storytelling and Stage Presence
topics: Structuring a personal story around a clear turning point and the lesson it left behind.
Using gestures that match the words instead of repeating one nervous movement.
Moving across the stage with purpose and standing still when the point matters most.
Shifting voice and posture lightly to suggest different characters inside a story.
Matching facial expression to the emotion of each part of the narrative.
Using a single prop or slide without letting it steal the audience's attention.
Adapting presence for a stage, for a classroom and for an online video call.

curriculum.title: Level 5: Impromptu and Thinking on Your Feet
topics: Answering a surprise topic with the point, reason, example and point structure.
Buying thinking time by restating the question in your own words before answering.
Speaking for a full minute on a random topic with no preparation at all.
Recovering smoothly after losing your place or forgetting a rehearsed line.
Handling audience questions, including one that you honestly cannot answer.
Reading the room and shortening or expanding a talk while still on your feet.
Practising the anchoring of an event, a vote of thanks and a short introduction of a guest.

curriculum.title: Level 6: Debate and Public Performance
topics: Framing a motion and defining its terms before arguing either side of it.
Building each argument as a claim, the evidence for it and the reasoning that ties the two together.
Listening actively and noting the opponent's exact words so that the reply is accurate.
Delivering a rebuttal that answers the opposition rather than restating your own case.
Offering and accepting points of information courteously under time pressure.
Preparing both the proposition and the opposition case for the same motion.
Performing a full assembly speech or an elocution piece before a live audience.
Reviewing recorded performances against a rubric of content, delivery and impact.

short_description: Live coaching in confidence, voice and stagecraft for young speakers.
description:
Online Public Speaking – Trial Class Plan (Session 1)

Duration: 60–75 MinutesMode: Online (Teacher + 5 Students)Theme: Introduction to Public Speaking & SWOT-Based Speaking Activity

Objective: Make students comfortable and start speaking immediately.
