Public speaking is a life skill. It helps in:

name: Spelling Competition
subtitle: Live spelling-bee coaching, from first phonics to the championship round.

curriculum.title: Level 1: Sounds and Spelling Patterns
topics: Matching every consonant and vowel sound in English to the letters that usually spell it.
Breaking a spoken word into syllables and clapping each beat before attempting to write it.
Spelling word families that share an ending pattern, such as -ack, -ing and -ight.
Using the split digraph, in which a silent e makes the vowel before it say its own name.
Telling apart long and short vowel sounds in pairs of words that look almost identical.
Spelling consonant blends such as str and spl alongside digraphs such as ch, sh and th.
Writing a short dictation every day and correcting it against the model answer.

curriculum.title: Level 2: Spelling Rules That Work
topics: Applying the i-before-e-except-after-c guideline and learning the words that break it.
Doubling the final consonant of a short word that ends in one vowel plus one consonant before a vowel suffix.
Deciding when the final silent e is dropped and when it is kept before a suffix.
Changing y to i before most suffixes and knowing when the y must stay, as it does before -ing.
Forming regular and irregular plurals, including nouns that end in f, o and y.
Using the British forms taught in Indian schools, such as colour, travelled and organisation.
Keeping practice and licence as the nouns and practise and license as the verbs.
Explaining aloud which rule was used rather than only producing the correct letters.

curriculum.title: Level 3: Roots, Prefixes and Suffixes
topics: Learning high-frequency Latin roots and using them to predict the meaning of unfamiliar words.
Learning Greek combining forms and spotting them inside science and medical vocabulary.
Building whole word families by adding several affixes to one shared root.
Using the negative prefixes in-, im-, il- and ir- correctly as they change before certain letters.
Recognising the suffixes that mark a word as a noun, an adjective or an adverb.
Spelling the weak schwa in an unstressed syllable by linking the word to a relative where that vowel is stressed.
Keeping a personal root notebook with at least three example words for every root learnt.

curriculum.title: Level 4: Tricky Words and Their Meanings
topics: Separating homophones such as stationary and stationery by holding on to their meanings.
Fixing frequently misspelt words such as accommodation, definitely and separate.
Spelling words English has taken from French, German, Spanish, Arabic and Japanese, and hearing what each origin sounds like.
Spelling everyday English words borrowed from Indian languages, such as bungalow, catamaran and jodhpurs.
Reading a dictionary entry for its pronunciation marks, its part of speech and its word origin.
Asking the pronouncer for the language of origin, the definition, the part of speech and a sentence.
Harvesting unfamiliar words from newspapers and storybooks into a weekly personal list.
Using a newly learnt word correctly in a sentence of your own to prove real understanding.

curriculum.title: Level 5: Contest Technique
topics: Practising the oral protocol of repeating the word, spelling it and then saying it once more.
Sounding each letter clearly and pausing between syllables even when under pressure.
Restarting a word cleanly where the rules allow, without changing any letter already given.
Preparing for written rounds such as dictation, jumbled letters and picture clues.
Answering meaning, usage and pronunciation rounds that go beyond plain spelling.
Settling microphone nerves with slow breathing and one fixed routine before every word.
Building a revision schedule that returns to missed words at steadily widening intervals.

curriculum.title: Level 6: Championship Practice
topics: Sitting timed mock rounds that copy a full elimination bee from the warm-up words to the final.
Working through graded lists that step up from class level to championship level.
Analysing every miss to decide whether the rule, the root or the sound caused it.
Running sudden-death drills against a partner with a strict five-second limit on each answer.
Attempting a never-seen word by reasoning from its roots, its origin and its stress pattern.
Warming up on competition day with a short familiar list rather than with new material.
Reviewing recorded practice for posture, clarity and pace at the microphone.

short_description: Live spelling-bee coaching, from first phonics to the championship round.

name: Bollywood Dance
subtitle: Personalised live Bollywood coaching, from basics to stage-ready.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Bollywood Foundations
topics: Warming up with joint rotations, gentle dynamic stretches and a short rhythm walk before every practice session
Counting a film song in eights and clapping along so that every step lands on the beat rather than behind it
Standing in the basic Bollywood posture with a lifted chest, soft knees and firmly grounded feet
Practising the thumka, the confident hip sway that gives Bollywood dance its playful signature
Shaping simple single-hand gestures, known as hastas or mudras in the classical forms film dance borrows from, and holding them cleanly at eye level
Coordinating one arm pattern with one footwork pattern without the two drifting apart
Dancing a short eight-count sequence to a medium-tempo film track entirely from memory
Letting the face join in the dance by holding a relaxed smile and steady focus towards the front

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Footwork, Grace and Expression
topics: Drilling flat-foot, half-toe and heel-toe footwork patterns at gradually increasing tempos
Rolling the chest and shoulders and dropping the hip on a count, the isolations that film choreography leans on most
Practising graceful wrist circles and finger extensions that finish off every arm line
Matching facial expression to the mood of a song, the film-dance cousin of classical abhinaya, moving between joyful, romantic and defiant
Learning to spot while turning so that a simple spin does not leave the dancer dizzy
Linking four eight-counts into one continuous phrase with clean transitions between them
Building stamina through a repeated cardio-style dance drill at the close of each session
Filming a short practice clip and reviewing it to catch dropped arms or rushed counts

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Folk Roots of Film Dance
topics: Bouncing on the balls of the feet with lifted, rolling shoulders in the high-energy Punjabi bhangra style that film songs draw on
Practising the circling steps and teen-taali clap patterns of Gujarati garba as they appear in festival numbers
Working with the grounded knees, quick footwork and expressive torso that characterise Maharashtrian lavani
Handling a dupatta or scarf so the fabric travels with the body rather than against it
Adjusting energy levels between a soft folk lyric and a high-octane celebration sequence
Understanding how film choreographers of the 1950s and 1960s reworked regional folk forms for the screen
Dancing a folk-flavoured routine in group formation while holding spacing with the dancers alongside
Keeping the breath steady through a fast folk sequence so the face stays relaxed throughout

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Street and Western Fusion
topics: Adding a hip hop bounce underneath familiar Bollywood arm patterns without losing the film-dance character
Practising sharp stops and freezes that punctuate a beat drop in a modern film song
Borrowing jazz kicks, chest lifts and long pointed lines for a contemporary film number
Sliding smoothly between a classical hand gesture and a street-style isolation inside one phrase
Working on partner changes and formation shifts used in large ensemble film sequences
Layering a slow lyrical section against a fast rhythmic section within a single routine
Strengthening the core and legs with conditioning drills that support jumps and level changes
Choosing which style suits a given track and explaining that choice to the tutor

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Choreography and Musicality
topics: Breaking a film song into its mukhda, antara and instrumental interlude before any steps are set
Setting original eight-counts to a film track chosen with the tutor and reworking them week by week
Using contrasting dynamics, sharp against smooth, so a routine does not read as one flat texture
Catching the accents of the dholak, tabla or drum machine as well as the phrasing of the singer
Designing entrances, exits and stage pathways for a small group of dancers
Teaching a self-made sequence back to the tutor clearly enough for it to be copied accurately
Reworking the same routine for a narrow school stage, a crowded wedding floor and an open terrace
Keeping a choreography notebook of counts, corrections and weekly rehearsal targets

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Performance and Showreel
topics: Rehearsing a full-length routine until it can be danced confidently without counting aloud
Choosing costume, hair and make-up that suit the character and era of the number
Settling nerves before going on with a fixed pre-show warm-up and a slow, counted breath
Projecting expression to the back of a hall and to a close camera lens in equal measure
Carrying on through a slip or a missed count while staying inside the mood of the song so the audience never sees it
Filming a routine in one unbroken take, since panels want to see stamina and consistency rather than edits
Working through a recorded performance review with the tutor and applying each correction in the next run
Building a three-routine set covering a classical-leaning number, a folk number and a modern film number

short_description: Personalised live Bollywood coaching, from basics to stage-ready.

name: Kuchipudi Dance
subtitle: Live one-to-one Kuchipudi classes, from adugulu to tarangam on the plate.

curriculum.title: Level 1 – Kuchipudi Foundations
topics: Settling into ardhamandali, the Kuchipudi half-sit, which is held more lightly and left more often than the deeper Bharatanatyam araimandi.
Practising the first set of adugulu, the basic steps, to spoken syllables at a slow and patient speed.
Performing the namaskaram and learning about the older stage-consecration ritual it comes from.
Clapping and counting the eight-beat adi talam and the six-beat rupaka talam before dancing to either of them.
Beginning the single-hand hastas and naming each one aloud as it is learnt.
Understanding that Kuchipudi began as a male dance-drama tradition in a village in coastal Andhra.
Finding the springy, travelling quality of Kuchipudi footwork instead of a purely grounded step.
Practising the quick weight shifts and small jumps on a wooden or sprung floor rather than on concrete, to protect the knees.

curriculum.title: Level 2 – Adugulu and Jathis
topics: Completing the second set of adugulu and joining them into sequences that travel right across the floor.
Dancing jathis in each of the five jaathis, from three-count tisra through to nine-count sankeerna.
Reciting the drum syllables aloud before dancing them, so the rhythm is understood rather than merely copied.
Adding the double-hand hastas and keeping them legible even while the body is still travelling.
Learning the drishti bhedas, the eye movements, and using them so the gaze follows the hand and never drifts.
Performing a short invocation to Ganapati, the ritual opening Kuchipudi keeps from its dance-drama purvaranga.
Wearing gajjelu, the Telugu ankle bells, and learning to still them through quiet expressive passages.
Dancing one jathi at two speeds and keeping the footwork equally clean when it doubles.

curriculum.title: Level 3 – Nritta Repertoire and Expression
topics: Learning a jathiswaram in which pure dance patterns are set to a Carnatic melody with no lyric at all.
Dancing a shabdam in which sung Telugu lines of praise alternate with brisk drum-syllable passages.
Learning to shift rasa inside a single line, since a Kuchipudi character often turns from pleading to anger mid-sentence.
Using the flowing torso and shoulder movement that separates Kuchipudi from the squarer southern styles.
Holding the sculpturesque poses that punctuate a Kuchipudi jathi, checking line and balance before any speed is added.
Working with a nattuvanar who both recites and conducts, and learning the cues that signal a repeat or a finish.
Reading a Telugu lyric beside its translation and choosing a gesture for each phrase.
Working up to a twenty-minute run of items without the ardhamandali lifting or the travelling steps shortening.

curriculum.title: Level 4 – Dance-Drama and Character
topics: Learning daruvu, the character-introduction songs through which each role enters a Kuchipudi drama.
Portraying the proud heroine Satyabhama, the role that anchors the traditional Andhra dance-drama repertoire.
Delivering sung or spoken Telugu dialogue, the vachika abhinaya that Kuchipudi kept from its theatre roots.
Switching between two characters within one scene through posture, gaze and rhythmic weight alone.
Improvising inside a dramatic scene so that a reaction can be stretched or cut according to how the audience responds.
Handling the long plait, the veil and the costume properties that traditional female roles require.
Understanding the all-male lineage of the form and how women came to dominate it in the last century.
Preparing a Telugu item together with its translation for examiners who expect the dancer to explain every line.

curriculum.title: Level 5 – Tarangam and Technical Mastery
topics: Learning to balance on the rim of a brass plate and shift weight without ever letting the plate tip.
Dancing a tarangam, travelling the plate across the floor in time with the mridangam.
Answering the mridangam's syllables with footwork taken on the plate itself, without stepping off it.
Balancing a water pot on the head while keeping the neck free enough to carry expression.
Dancing one jathi in tisra gati and then in chatusra gati so the same phrase reshapes itself against the same talam.
Studying how Narayana Teertha, a seventeenth-century saint-composer of Andhra, shaped the devotional repertoire that gives tarangam its name.
Sustaining abhinaya through the balance so the face keeps telling the story while the feet are on the rim.
Strengthening the feet, ankles and core specifically for plate work and sustained balance.

curriculum.title: Level 6 – Solo Margam and Performance
topics: Assembling a recital that keeps Kuchipudi's double character, moving from pure dance through a dramatic daruvu to a plate item.
Dancing a tillana as the closing item, snapping into each sculptural pose exactly on the beat.
Rehearsing with mridangam, violin and vocalist while a nattuvanar sets the tempo from the cymbals.
Deciding whether an item is stronger as a solo or as a scene with a second dancer, since the tradition allows both.
Speaking the Telugu of the sung text well enough to introduce and translate each item for an audience that does not know the language.
Budgeting a debut recital in rupees, covering musicians, hall hire, costume, the plate and pot, and photography.
Filming a recital and cutting a showreel that shows both the tarangam and a quiet expressive passage.
Mapping the festival, teaching and dance-company routes open to Kuchipudi dancers in India today.

short_description: Live one-to-one Kuchipudi classes, from adugulu to tarangam on the plate.

name: Bharatnatyam Dance
subtitle: Live one-to-one Bharatanatyam classes, from araimandi to arangetram.

curriculum.title: Level 1 – Foundations of Bharatanatyam
topics: Settling into araimandi, the half-sitting posture, and holding it comfortably with the arms level at the shoulders.
Practising tatta adavu, tapping the floor in the half-sit across all three speeds without ever rising out of the sit.
Learning natta adavu with its stretched leg and heel contact while the torso stays completely still.
Reciting the sollukattu syllables aloud while stepping, so that the mouth and the feet agree on the rhythm.
Recognising the eight-beat adi talam by clapping and counting a full cycle before any movement is added.
Beginning the asamyuta hastas of the Abhinaya Darpana, starting with pataka, tripataka and ardhapataka.
Performing the namaskaram that greets the earth, the guru and the audience at the start and close of every class.
Warming up the ankles, knees and hips safely at home so that daily half-sitting never strains the joints.

curriculum.title: Level 2 – Adavu Vocabulary and Rhythm
topics: Adding visharu and tattimettu adavus, coordinating the swing of the arms with heel-and-toe contact.
Practising kudittametta adavu, where a small spring is followed by a clean heel strike back in the half-sit.
Working through mettu and sarikkal adavus, sliding one foot outward while the body weight stays centred.
Joining adavus into short korvais that begin and land exactly on the first beat of the adi talam cycle.
Completing the twenty-eight single-hand hastas and beginning the samyuta hastas that use both palms together.
Clapping out the five jaathis — tisra, chatusra, khanda, misra and sankeerna — as three, four, five, seven and nine counts.
Dancing a short pushpanjali, the flower offering, built entirely from the adavus learnt so far.
Tying on salangai for the first time and adjusting the strap so the bells sound cleanly on every strike.

curriculum.title: Level 3 – Nritta into Nritya
topics: Completing the adavu families with mandi, murka, tirmanam and katti adavus at all three speeds.
Learning an alarippu, the pure-dance opening that wakes the body outward from the eyes down to the feet.
Dancing a jatiswaram, in which adavu patterns are set to a Carnatic melody with no sung text at all.
Introducing the nine rasas and practising each one in the mirror using only the eyes and the eyebrows.
Drilling the shirobheda, drishtibheda and grivabheda — the head, eye and neck movements of the treatises — as daily exercises.
Reading sollukattu notation so that a new korvai can be learnt from written syllables before it is demonstrated.
Using the samyuta hastas inside a danced phrase to name gods, animals and family relationships.
Building the stamina to work continuously in araimandi for ten minutes without the knees creeping upward.

curriculum.title: Level 4 – Abhinaya and Early Repertoire
topics: Learning a shabdam, the first item in which sung words and rhythmic passages alternate inside one piece.
Interpreting a Tamil or Telugu devotional lyric line by line and choosing a gesture for each word.
Practising sanchari bhava, stretching a single line of text into a short improvised story without losing the lyric.
Distinguishing natyadharmi from lokadharmi so that gesture reads as stylised dance rather than literal mime.
Studying the eight nayika types and the moods a lyric may ask the dancer to inhabit.
Dancing to live nattuvangam and picking up a change of tempo from the cymbals without looking down at the nattuvanar.
Rehearsing entrances, exits and stage positions for a proscenium stage rather than a square practice room.
Sitting a mock graded examination with set adavus, one prepared item and viva questions on talam and hasta names.

curriculum.title: Level 5 – Varnam and Advanced Practice
topics: Learning a varnam, the long centrepiece that alternates dense jathis with sustained expressive passages.
Pacing breath, energy and the depth of the half-sit so that a thirty- to forty-minute item can be sustained.
Handling trikala jathis, dancing one phrase at single, double and quadruple speed in immediate succession.
Working on a padam or a javali, where stillness and the eyes carry far more weight than the feet do.
Choreographing an original korvai and checking that its three-fold ending lands on the first beat of the cycle.
Studying how the form moved from temple and court practice onto the concert stage during the twentieth century.
Managing costume, pleated fan, temple jewellery and hair so that dressing for a show takes under an hour.
Recording practice and self-correcting alignment, line and finish frame by frame between lessons.

curriculum.title: Level 6 – Margam and Arangetram Preparation
topics: Assembling a full margam that runs in order from the invocation and alarippu through the varnam to the closing mangalam.
Dancing a tillana, the brisk Carnatic finale built on a chain of sculpturesque poses.
Rehearsing with nattuvanar, vocalist, mridangam and violin, and holding the ensemble together when the tempo shifts.
Pacing a two-hour arangetram, deciding where the costume changes fall and where the interval belongs.
Introducing each item from the stage in about a minute, naming its talam and raga and summarising its lyric.
Managing performance nerves with breath work, visualisation and a fixed routine on the day itself.
Costing an arangetram honestly in rupees, from the orchestra's fees and hall hire to costume and invitations.
Assembling recital footage, stage photographs and a written dance biography into a portfolio for auditions.

name: Kathak Dance
subtitle: Live one-to-one Kathak training, from tatkaar basics to a full solo recital.

curriculum.title: Level 1 – First Steps in Kathak
topics: Standing in the upright Kathak posture with a long spine, soft knees and level shoulders, with no half-sit at all.
Practising basic tatkaar, the flat-footed footwork of Kathak, slowly inside the sixteen-beat teentaal.
Counting a teentaal cycle aloud and locating the sam, the taalis and the khaali by clapping.
Learning both the vandana and the salaami with which Kathak dancers greet the stage and the audience.
Shaping simple hastak, the flowing arm and wrist patterns that frame every footwork phrase.
Reciting rhythmic bols clearly and in time before attempting to dance a single one of them.
Strengthening the ankles and calves so that flat-footed footwork can be sustained without pain.
Tying ghungroo correctly and learning to keep them completely silent whenever the dance asks for stillness.

curriculum.title: Level 2 – Tatkaar, Chakkars and Short Compositions
topics: Raising tatkaar through vilambit, madhya and drut laya without losing clarity in the feet.
Learning the basic chakkar, turning on the ball of the foot with the head carried in line with the body rather than snapping round to a spot as a ballet dancer would.
Performing thaat, the slow opening section in which only the wrists, neck and eyebrows move.
Dancing a simple tihai that states one phrase three times and lands precisely on the sam.
Learning short todas and tukras and reciting them in padhant before dancing a step of them.
Practising layakari by dancing the same tatkaar first in dugun and then in chaugun.
Adding the small head and eye accents that give a Kathak phrase its characteristic finish.
Placing the body weight correctly through a turn so that the spin stops cleanly and on the beat.

curriculum.title: Level 3 – Aamad, Paran and Gharana Style
topics: Learning an aamad, the formal entry composition whose name means arrival and which announces the dancer.
Dancing a paran built on pakhawaj syllables, with the heavier attack that drum demands.
Adding chakkardar todas, in which a whole composition repeats three times and each repeat carries spins.
Comparing the delicate Lucknow treatment of a phrase with the vigorous, footwork-heavy Jaipur treatment of the same phrase.
Working in a second taal, either the ten-beat jhaptaal or the twelve-beat ektaal.
Reciting compositions unaccompanied in padhant with the correct weight placed on each syllable.
Answering a short tabla phrase by dancing its bols straight back, the first taste of dialogue with the drummer.
Studying how Kathak passed from the kathakars' temple storytelling into the Mughal courts and was reshaped there.

curriculum.title: Level 4 – Abhinaya and Gat
topics: Learning gat nikas, the stylised walks that show a character arriving through gait, veil and glance.
Performing gat bhaav, mimed episodes told entirely through gesture and expression with no sung words at all.
Interpreting a thumri line so that one phrase can be shown three convincingly different ways in a row.
Carrying bhaav in the eyes and eyebrows while the feet keep an entirely independent rhythm underneath.
Handling the odhni so that the fabric moves with the character instead of fighting against her.
Setting a short bhajan to simple movement and sustaining one mood from its first line to its last.
Dancing to live tabla and recovering gracefully whenever the accompanist shifts the laya without warning.
Sitting a mock Kathak grade of the kind Gandharva Mahavidyalaya conducts, where a composition must be recited, danced and then explained aloud.

curriculum.title: Level 5 – Speed, Layakari and Solo Craft
topics: Sustaining a long run of chakkars and stopping the final spin exactly on the sam.
Building complex layakari including tigun, aad and kuaad against a steady tabla cycle.
Composing an original toda and checking that its tihai resolves on the sam rather than a beat either side of it.
Dancing a kavitt, a short poem in which every line is both recited aloud and shown in movement.
Improvising a sawal-jawab exchange with the tabla player across several complete cycles.
Structuring a solo so that nritta and abhinaya alternate and the energy keeps climbing towards the end.
Conditioning the knees, ankles and lower back to survive long spells of fast flat-footed footwork.
Stringing a heavier set of ghungroo and judging when the ankles are strong enough to carry the extra weight.

curriculum.title: Level 6 – Full Recital and Performance
topics: Building a complete solo that runs from vandana through thaat and aamad into todas, tukras and a fast close.
Dancing a tarana, the Hindustani finale in which footwork and chakkars carry the whole item with no story to lean on.
Rehearsing with live tabla and sarangi or harmonium, cueing the accompanists with a glance rather than a stop.
Improvising in front of an audience by taking a bol the tabla player offers and answering it unrehearsed.
Reading a small mehfil-style room differently from a large proscenium stage and scaling the movement to each.
Working out an honest rupee budget for accompanists, costume, ghungroo and hall hire for a debut recital.
Filming from a fixed wide angle that keeps the feet in frame, then cutting a two-minute showreel from it.
Understanding what teaching, festival and collaborative work is realistically open to a Kathak dancer in India.

name: Hip Hop Dance
subtitle: Live one-to-one hip hop coaching, from grooves to freestyle.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Groove and Bounce Foundations
topics: Finding the bounce and the rock, the two grooves that sit underneath almost every hip hop step
Warming up the joints and spine with mobility drills that protect the knees and lower back
Hearing where the kick, the snare and the offbeat fall inside a track and stepping to each in turn
Standing in a relaxed, grounded stance with the weight held over the balls of the feet
Practising the social party dances that hip hop grew out of, which build rhythm and confidence quickly
Stepping in time to a slowed-down track and then repeating the same step at full tempo
Holding a single groove for a full minute without the shoulders creeping upwards
Learning cypher etiquette, including sharing the floor and hyping up whoever is dancing

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Toprock and Footwork
topics: Building a basic toprock, the upright breaking step, that travels forwards, backwards and to either side
Adding arm swings and cross-body reaches that match the weight of the footwork below
Practising kick-steps, side steps and shuffle patterns cleanly at a moderate tempo
Dropping from standing towards the floor and rising again under control, the go-down that links toprock to floor material
Drilling a footwork sequence against a metronome to iron out uneven timing
Linking two contrasting footwork patterns together with a smooth transition step
Conditioning the ankles and calves so they absorb repeated bounce without strain
Performing a thirty-second toprock phrase from memory in front of the tutor

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Isolations, Popping and Locking
topics: Popping cleanly by contracting and releasing one muscle group on a chosen beat, the hit that gives the style its name
Isolating head, ribcage and hips so a hit lands in one body part while everything else stays quiet
Sending a wave through both arms and across the chest with even, unbroken travel
Learning the wrist rolls, points and deliberate pauses of locking, a Californian funk style rather than a form of breaking
Freezing sharply into a shape and holding it without wobble for a full count
Alternating between robotic sharpness and loose relaxation inside a single phrase
Slowing recorded footage down to check each hit against the actual drum sound
Joining eight counts of popping to eight counts of locking in one short routine

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Freestyle and Musicality
topics: Improvising continuously for one minute without repeating the same step twice
Choosing whether to dance to the drums, the bass line or the vocal within the same track
Responding to a break or a drop with a matching change in body dynamics
Entering and leaving a cypher confidently while reading the energy of the circle
Building a personal vocabulary of five signature moves that feel natural to the body
Practising call-and-response exchanges with the tutor over a live beat
Using pauses and stillness as deliberate choices rather than moments of hesitation
Reviewing recorded freestyles to spot habits and gaps in the movement range

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Choreography and Crew Work
topics: Building a routine phrase by phrase from a chosen instrumental and tightening it session by session
Counting a routine aloud accurately enough for another dancer to learn it from the count alone
Designing staggers, canons and level changes for a crew of four to eight dancers
Timing a unison section so that every dancer strikes the same accent together
Applying contrasting textures of sharp, sustained and swung movement inside one piece
Rehearsing formation changes so that the travel between shapes looks intentional
Building the stamina to run a two-minute routine twice with no drop in quality
Giving and receiving constructive corrections during a crew rehearsal

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Battle, Stage and Showreel
topics: Planning a battle round that opens strongly, builds through the middle and closes on a clear final hit
Handling a one-on-one round to an unfamiliar track without freezing up
Reading how judges and the crowd respond to a round and adjusting what comes next
Following a structured warm-up before any battle or recording session
Filming a showreel from a low, wide angle that keeps footwork and floor material visible
Tracing breaking back to Bronx block parties and popping and locking back to Californian funk scenes so each style is credited accurately
Carrying on through a mid-round mistake by staying in character until the next eight begins
Assembling a portfolio of freestyle footage, set choreography and crew work for auditions

name: Zumba Dance
subtitle: Live Latin-rhythm dance-fitness sessions for stamina, coordination and everyday fitness.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Dance-Fitness Basics and Safe Movement
topics: Warming up the hips, knees, ankles and spine thoroughly before the first cardio track begins
Learning the basic salsa side step, a Cuban-rooted quick-quick-slow weight change, with the knees kept soft throughout
Practising the merengue march, a Dominican two-step in which the hips move with each weight change rather than against it
Marching on the spot to raise the heart rate gently and checking effort using the talk test
Understanding how a session alternates higher and lower intensity songs to train the heart
Drinking water at planned points and recognising the signals that mean it is time to ease off
Cooling down with slow stretches for the calves, hamstrings and lower back
Completing a shortened thirty-minute session from warm-up right through to cool-down

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Latin Rhythms and Cardio Stamina
topics: Adding the Colombian cumbia step, travelling back and forward, while the upper body stays relaxed
Practising grounded reggaeton steps built on the Puerto Rican dembow rhythm to strengthen the hips and thighs
Holding a steady working pace across three consecutive songs without stopping
Using overhead arm patterns to lift the heart rate without adding any joint impact
Rating effort on a simple perceived-exertion scale after each track and noting the score
Swapping any jump for a low-impact step-out whenever the knees or hips feel loaded
Recovering the breath during the slower song so that the next high-intensity song can be worked hard
Completing a full forty-five-minute session and logging honestly how it felt afterwards

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Interval Work and Toning
topics: Working through a high-and-low interval sequence that raises and drops the heart rate deliberately
Adding light resistance to arm-focused tracks while keeping the shoulders down and the elbows soft
Strengthening the core with standing oblique and abdominal patterns set to music
Folding squat and lunge variations into Latin steps to build lower-body endurance
Treating the calorie figures shown by apps and trackers as rough estimates rather than exact measurements
Balancing dance-fitness sessions with rest days so that the knees and ankles are not overused
Measuring progress with simple markers such as resting heart rate and how quickly the breath settles after a hard track
Holding good posture through the final third of a session when fatigue begins to set in

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Low-Impact and Inclusive Options
topics: Converting every core step into a low-impact version that keeps one foot on the floor
Practising a seated, chair-supported routine suitable for someone with limited mobility
Slowing the tempo for older participants while keeping the workout genuinely effective
Adapting movement sensibly for someone returning after a knee, hip or back complaint, staying within whatever their clinician has advised
Cueing intensity choices so that everyone in a mixed group can pick their own level within a single track
Watching for warning signs such as breathlessness that will not settle, dizziness or sharp joint pain, and stopping when they appear
Building a gentle thirty-minute session plan suitable for a mixed-ability family group
Recognising when a participant should be encouraged to seek medical clearance before continuing

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Session Design and Leading a Group
topics: Sequencing a full sixty-minute playlist that climbs, peaks and cools along a planned curve
Choreographing simple repeatable patterns that a first-timer can pick up within a single chorus
Cueing with clear hand signals and short verbal calls so that the music, not the talking, leads the room
Setting up a home or hall space safely with attention to flooring, ventilation and spacing between participants
Leading a mixed group while scanning the room and correcting unsafe knee and back alignment
Understanding that Zumba is a licensed brand and that teaching classes under that name requires official instructor certification, while these skills apply to any Latin dance-fitness session
Running a practice session for friends or family and gathering honest feedback afterwards
Planning an eight-week personal fitness block with measurable stamina and consistency goals

name: Western Dance
subtitle: Live coaching in jazz, contemporary and ballet basics, at your pace.

curriculum.title: Level 1 — Western Dance Foundations
topics: Warming up with a structured routine that raises the pulse and mobilises every major joint
Standing in correct alignment with a lengthened spine, level hips and relaxed shoulders
Hearing where an eight-count phrase begins and ends, and finishing a movement on the last count rather than after it
Walking, running and skipping across the floor in time with the music
Learning parallel and turned-out foot positions and feeling how turnout comes from the hip rather than the knee
Discovering how one body part can move while the rest stays still, starting with the head and shoulders
Balancing on one leg for a held count with the supporting knee tracking over the toes
Cooling down with slow stretches and understanding why they belong at the end of a class rather than the start

curriculum.title: Level 2 — Ballet Basics at the Barre
topics: Learning the five positions of the feet and holding each one with an honest turnout rather than a forced one
Practising demi-plié with the heels staying on the floor, and grand plié where the heels release in every position except second
Extending the working leg in battement tendu to the front, side and back without letting the weight shift
Rising through relevé to demi-pointe and lowering with control to build strength through the ankles
Carrying the arms through the basic port de bras positions with a soft, supported elbow line
Using the French vocabulary of ballet accurately, since each term names the exact movement being asked for
Travelling a simple chassé and pas de bourrée sequence across the room
Performing a short barre and centre sequence assessed for line, control and musicality

curriculum.title: Level 3 — Jazz Technique and Style
topics: Drilling sharp ribcage and hip isolations against a still, quiet lower body
Practising the jazz square, kick-ball-change and pivot turn until they become automatic
Learning a single pirouette from fourth position with a reliable spot on a fixed point
Adding leaps and jumps that land through a controlled plié so the knees are protected
Using contrasting dynamics of attack and suspension inside a single jazz phrase
Working on performance quality, including projection and confident eye focus
Stretching for hip and hamstring range to support higher kicks over the coming weeks
Dancing a one-minute jazz combination cleanly and confidently from memory

curriculum.title: Level 4 — Contemporary and Floorwork
topics: Exploring contraction and release through the spine, the principle Martha Graham built her technique around
Falling and recovering safely so that weight can be given to the floor without impact
Rolling, sliding and rising through floorwork sequences without hesitation
Using the breath to shape the length and quality of a movement phrase
Improvising to a set task, such as letting one body part lead every change of direction
Building fluid transitions that hide the join between standing and floor material
Turning a personal idea or image into a thirty-second movement study
Conditioning the core and back with exercises that support off-balance work

curriculum.title: Level 5 — Composition, Musicality and Partner Work
topics: Shaping a two-minute improvisation across changing music so that the material develops instead of circling back
Blending ballet line, contemporary weight and jazz attack within one continuous routine
Setting a phrase first against the melodic line and then against the underlying pulse, and noticing how differently the same steps read
Developing a short motif by changing its size, speed and direction rather than inventing new steps
Building unison, canon and counterpoint sections for a small group of dancers
Rehearsing with a partner and matching timing, height and quality of movement
Sharing weight safely with a partner through simple counterbalances and supported leans
Marking a piece through at half energy to fix spacing without exhausting the body

curriculum.title: Level 6 — Solo Performance and Audition Portfolio
topics: Polishing a full-length solo until it can be performed twice in a row with no loss of quality
Preparing a contrasting pair of pieces, one technical and one expressive, for audition use
Choosing costume that suits each style and lets the line of the body read clearly from the audience
Building an audition-day routine that covers arrival, warm-up, marking through and the waiting time in between
Understanding how graded dance examinations are structured, so the learner can decide whether to enter for an early grade with a recognised examination board
Recording an audition reel that opens with a clear spoken slate of name, age and training background
Working from written tutor feedback across a block of rehearsals and tracking which corrections have held
Presenting a final performance to an invited audience or to camera with full commitment

name: Spanish
subtitle: Live one-to-one Spanish coaching from first words to DELE B2.

curriculum.title: Level 1 - Spanish Sounds and First Conversations
topics: Starting from no previous Spanish and reading the language aloud in the first lesson, because its five vowels keep the same pure sound wherever they fall.
Separating the single tapped r of pero from the rolled rr of perro until the two stop sounding alike.
Greeting people, introducing yourself and spelling your name aloud with the Spanish alphabet, including the letter enye.
Learning why every noun carries a gender and attaching el, la, los or las to each new word as you meet it.
Conjugating regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs in the present tense to describe an ordinary day at home and at school.
Deciding between ser and estar by asking whether you are naming what something is or describing the state it is in.
Counting to a hundred, giving your age with tener rather than with the verb to be, and quoting a price so you can set euros or pesos against rupees.

curriculum.title: Level 2 - Talking About Your World
topics: Placing adjectives after the noun as Spanish usually does, making them agree in gender and number, and noticing the few such as gran or viejo that change meaning when they move in front.
Using stem-changing verbs such as querer, poder and preferir, where the vowel shifts in every form except nosotros and vosotros.
Making plans with ir a followed by an infinitive, keeping the a that English drops and that French does not use at all.
Telling the time from a twenty-four hour timetable and describing your week in order.
Ordering food, bargaining in a market and making a polite complaint using usted rather than tu.
Narrating finished events in the preterito indefinido, beginning with regular verbs and the common irregulars ir, ser and hacer, two of which share the same forms.
Replacing repeated nouns with direct and indirect object pronouns, placing them before the verb or attached to an infinitive.
Writing a short personal message with the opening question and exclamation marks that Spanish turns upside down, and with the accent that separates si from yes.

curriculum.title: Level 3 - Past, Habit and Opinion
topics: Choosing between the preterito indefinido and the imperfecto so that a finished event and the background it happened against stay apart.
Using reflexive verbs for daily routine, for changes of mood and for actions you carry out on yourself.
Comparing things with mas que, menos que and tan como, and forming superlatives including the -isimo ending.
Giving instructions and advice with affirmative commands and with the negative forms that borrow their endings from the subjunctive.
Handling health, travel and directions in role-play drawn from real situations in Spain and in Latin America.
Listening to a short recorded announcement or dialogue once and answering questions on it under time pressure.
Completing the two writing tasks the DELE A2 paper sets inside its fifty minutes.
Rehearsing the DELE A2 speaking test, which you sit alone with an examiner rather than with another candidate.

curriculum.title: Level 4 - The Subjunctive and Independent Spanish
topics: Forming the present subjunctive and recognising the wish, doubt, emotion and influence that trigger it.
Stating an opinion and disagreeing politely in a discussion that runs for several minutes without dropping into English.
Using the preterito perfecto to tie recent events to now, and noticing that much of Latin America prefers the simple past where Spain would not.
Speculating, promising and supposing with the future and conditional, including the future used for guesswork about the present moment.
Reading an opinion column and restating its argument in your own Spanish instead of translating it.
Writing a formal email of enquiry or complaint with the register, opening and closing formulae Spanish correspondence expects.
Tracking the differences between peninsular and American Spanish in vocabulary, in the seseo pronunciation of c and z, and in vosotros against ustedes.
Building a personal vocabulary bank around a subject you care about and revising it on a spaced schedule.

curriculum.title: Level 5 - Argument and Nuance
topics: Using the imperfect subjunctive with si clauses to talk about unreal, regretted and imagined situations.
Structuring a spoken argument with connectors that signal contrast, cause and conclusion.
Avoiding the agent with the passive, with impersonal se and with the third person plural that Spanish often prefers to either.
Following film and radio across accents, from Caribbean speech that swallows the s to the River Plate pronunciation of ll and y.
Writing a balanced argument of roughly one hundred and fifty to one hundred and eighty words, the length the DELE B2 writing tasks ask for.
Recognising register and idiom so your Spanish sounds neither textbook-stiff nor unintentionally rude.
Recording yourself, reading the transcript back with your tutor and fixing the English vowel sounds and stress patterns that keep returning.

curriculum.title: Level 6 - Certification and Working Spanish
topics: Sitting full timed DELE B2 mocks and learning that the four papers are marked in two groups, both of which must be cleared separately.
Preparing a proposal in the twenty minutes allowed and then defending it in conversation with the examiner.
Interpreting short simulated meetings and telephone calls in both directions between English and Spanish.
Writing a Spanish curriculum and carta de presentacion aimed at travel, translation or customer-facing work.
Handling professional situations such as negotiating a price, chairing a call and explaining a delay to a client.
Reading a short literary extract and discussing how the writer handles tense and imagery, setting a peninsular voice beside a Latin American one.
Collecting your best spoken and written work into a portfolio for employers, alongside a DELE diploma that never expires.
Planning the independent reading and listening that keeps your Spanish improving while the result is awaited.

name: French
subtitle: Live one-to-one French coaching, first sounds to DELF B2 confidence.

curriculum.title: Level 1 - French Sounds and Survival Phrases
topics: Beginning with no French at all and learning to read it aloud, including the final consonants that stay silent.
Producing the nasal vowels in on, an and in without letting an n or m escape at the end, and hearing how un has merged with in for most speakers today.
Choosing between tu and vous for the person in front of you and understanding what the choice signals about the relationship.
Learning each noun with its article from the very first word, since gender cannot be predicted from meaning.
Conjugating etre, avoir and the regular -er verbs to talk about yourself and your family.
Making the liaison that joins les to amis so that spoken French runs together instead of word by word.
Counting past sixty, where French switches to soixante-dix, quatre-vingts and quatre-vingt-dix, and meeting the septante and nonante used in Belgium and Switzerland.
Asking a question in three ways, by intonation, with est-ce que and by inverting the verb and the subject.

curriculum.title: Level 2 - Daily Life in French
topics: Placing most adjectives after the noun while learning the short set of beauty, age, goodness and size words that come before it.
Using -ir and -re verbs alongside the irregulars aller, faire, venir and pouvoir.
Talking about what you did in the passe compose, choosing between avoir and etre and making the agreement that etre brings with it.
Saying some bread and no sugar accurately with partitive articles and with the de that replaces them after a negative.
Shopping, ordering a meal and asking for directions in role-play, using on where English would say we.
Writing a short message with the accents that change meaning, such as a against a grave and ou against ou with an accent, and with the cedilla.
Following slow, clear station and airport announcements and picking out times, platforms and gate numbers.

curriculum.title: Level 3 - Narrating and Describing
topics: Contrasting the imparfait with the passe compose so that a scene can be set before the story is allowed to move.
Replacing repeated nouns with object pronouns and with y and en, and ordering them correctly when two appear together.
Talking about immediate plans with the futur proche and later intentions with the futur simple.
Giving instructions with the imperative and expressing obligation with il faut and devoir.
Comparing and ranking things with plus, moins, aussi and the superlative forms.
Writing the two short texts of at least sixty words each that the DELF A2 paper sets.
Rehearsing the DELF A2 oral, where you face the examiner alone through a guided interview, an exchange of information and a role-play.
Describing a photograph or a familiar place for a full minute without stopping to translate from English.

curriculum.title: Level 4 - Opinion and the Subjunctive
topics: Forming the present subjunctive and recognising the expressions of will, emotion and doubt that call for it.
Linking longer sentences with qui, que, dont and ou, and working out which one the following clause actually needs.
Reporting what somebody else said with the shift of tense, pronoun and time expression that goes with it.
Debating for several minutes, conceding a point and disagreeing without giving offence.
Reading the francophone press from Quebec, West Africa and the Maghreb as well as from France and summarising the writer's position.
Writing a formal letter with the elaborate closing formula French correspondence still expects.
Hearing verlan and the dropped ne of casual speech, and judging when not to use either yourself.

curriculum.title: Level 5 - Structured Argument
topics: Building an argument in the thesis, antithesis and synthesis plan that French teachers and examiners expect.
Hypothesising, reproaching and softening a request with the conditional and with si clauses.
Using the passive and nominalisation, and recognising the passe simple when you meet it in print rather than in speech.
Taking usable notes from unscripted radio discussion running at natural pace.
Deploying the connectors that mark concession, cause, consequence and reformulation across a written paragraph.
Writing the argued position of at least two hundred and fifty words that the DELF B2 written paper requires.
Recording yourself to check the nasal vowels, the liaisons and the unstable e that French speakers drop.

curriculum.title: Level 6 - Certification and Professional French
topics: Sitting complete DELF B2 mocks, where each of the four skills carries twenty-five marks and a minimum score is needed in every one of them.
Preparing a short trigger article in thirty minutes and then defending a point of view on it under questioning.
Writing a French CV and the lettre de motivation that an employer or university reads before it.
Getting through French administrative exchanges such as an enrolment, a bank appointment and a request for a document.
Reading a journalistic or literary extract closely and commenting on its style as a French explication de texte would.
Learning why DELF and DALF diplomas are valid for life while the TCF and TEF tests expire after two years.
Collecting written pieces and recordings into a dossier you can put in front of a Campus France adviser or an employer.
Setting up a reading and listening habit in French that carries on after the last lesson.
