name: German
subtitle: Live one-to-one German coaching, from der-die-das to Goethe B2.

curriculum.title: Level 1 - German Sounds and First Sentences
topics: Reading German aloud from the first lesson with no prior knowledge, since its spelling maps onto sound far more regularly than English spelling does.
Producing the umlaut vowels and separating the soft ch of ich from the hard ch of Buch.
Learning every noun with its article, because der, die and das cannot be guessed from meaning, and capitalising every noun in writing.
Conjugating regular verbs together with sein and haben in the present tense.
Keeping the conjugated verb in second position whatever you choose to put first in the sentence.
Meeting the nominative and accusative cases through simple subject and object sentences.
Counting in German, where twenty-one is spoken as one-and-twenty, and reading halb drei as half past two rather than half past three.

curriculum.title: Level 2 - Cases and Everyday German
topics: Adding the dative for indirect objects and for the prepositions such as mit, nach and von that always demand it.
Choosing accusative or dative after a two-way preposition by asking whether the phrase answers wohin or wo, not simply whether anyone is moving.
Saying what you can, must, want and are allowed to do with the modal verbs and the infinitive they send to the end of the clause.
Splitting separable verbs so the prefix lands at the end, and rejoining them inside a subordinate clause.
Talking about the past with the perfect tense and choosing haben or sein as its auxiliary.
Breaking a long compound noun into its parts and reading the last element as the one that carries both the gender and the core meaning.
Making appointments, buying tickets and asking for help in role-play with your tutor.

curriculum.title: Level 3 - Building Longer Sentences
topics: Sending the verb to the end of clauses opened by weil, dass, wenn and ob, while keeping it second after deshalb and trotzdem.
Adding adjective endings that answer to the article, the gender and the case at once, through the strong, weak and mixed patterns.
Using the Praeteritum of common verbs for written narrative while everyday speech keeps the perfect tense.
Handling reflexive verbs and the fixed prepositions that particular verbs insist upon.
Describing your town, your studies and your plans in a connected two-minute turn.
Completing the two short writing tasks of the Goethe A2 paper inside its thirty minutes.
Rehearsing the Goethe A2 speaking module, which unlike most other exams you sit with a partner candidate.

curriculum.title: Level 4 - Independent German
topics: Completing the case system with the genitive and prepositions such as waehrend and wegen, while noticing that speech often replaces it with von and the dative.
Making polite requests, giving advice and imagining outcomes with Konjunktiv II, the second subjunctive.
Building relative clauses whose pronoun changes with gender, number and case and which push the verb to the end.
Expressing purpose, result and concession with um zu, damit, sodass and obwohl.
Reading a factual article and summarising it in German instead of translating it word by word.
Giving a short prepared talk on a familiar subject and taking unrehearsed questions on it.
Writing a semi-formal letter with the correct salutation, paragraphing and sign-off.
Recognising Austrian and Swiss usage in recorded and printed material, from Jaenner for January to the Swiss habit of writing ss where Germany writes the sharp s.

curriculum.title: Level 5 - Formal and Analytical German
topics: Using the passive in its present, past and modal forms and telling the process passive apart from the state passive.
Unpacking the extended participial phrases that compress a whole relative clause in front of a noun in academic writing.
Reporting speech with Konjunktiv I, the form German journalism uses to keep its distance from a claim.
Debating a contested subject with structured arguments, supporting evidence and answers to the other side.
Taking usable notes from lectures, interviews and news bulletins running at natural speed.
Writing a structured opinion piece of about two hundred and fifty words with clear paragraphing.
Growing vocabulary through word families, separable and inseparable prefixes and the logic of compounding.

curriculum.title: Level 6 - Certification and Working German
topics: Sitting the four Goethe B2 modules as timed mocks, each passed at sixty per cent and each retakable on its own.
Presenting a topic and then discussing it with a partner candidate, which is how the B2 speaking module actually runs.
Writing a tabular Lebenslauf and an Anschreiben in the layout German employers expect, dated and signed.
Handling professional exchanges such as a technical query, a service complaint and a project update.
Understanding that B2 opens apprenticeships and many jobs while degree admission usually asks for C1 evidence such as TestDaF or the DSH.
Reading a demanding extract and following its argument through the long nested sentences German permits.
Assembling recordings and written work into a portfolio, noting that institutions often want a certificate issued within the last two years even though Goethe certificates do not expire.
Setting a self-study routine of reading, podcasts and conversation that keeps the German alive after the course ends.

short_description: Live one-to-one German coaching, from der-die-das to Goethe B2.

name: Mandarin
subtitle: Live one-to-one Mandarin coaching, from tones to HSK certification.

curriculum.title: Level 1 - Tones, Pinyin and First Words
topics: Starting with no Chinese at all and hearing the four tones and the neutral tone until they stop sounding alike.
Reading pinyin accurately, including the initials and finals such as zh, q, x and the u with two dots that English has no use for.
Greeting people, introducing yourself and exchanging basic personal information.
Counting, giving dates and putting the correct measure word between a number and a noun.
Building simple statements in subject, verb and object order while noticing how often Chinese puts the topic first instead.
Asking questions with the particle ma or with the verb-not-verb pattern, since Chinese never inverts anything.
Writing your first characters in the correct stroke order with balanced proportions.
Practising tone pairs aloud so that a third tone before another third tone changes as it should.

curriculum.title: Level 2 - Characters and Daily Conversation
topics: Learning the common radicals so that a new character offers a clue to its meaning or its sound.
Reaching a working set of everyday characters you can recognise on sight and also write by hand.
Talking about time, weather, family and routine, placing time words before the verb as Chinese requires.
Marking a completed action and a changed situation with the two distinct uses of the particle le.
Shopping and bargaining in role-play, saying prices with the spoken kuai and mao rather than the written yuan and jiao.
Typing Chinese on a phone and a laptop with a pinyin input method and picking the right character from the candidate list.
Telling simplified characters from traditional ones and knowing where each of them is used.

curriculum.title: Level 3 - Connected Speech and Reading
topics: Saying how an action turned out with resultative complements and where it went with directional ones.
Comparing two things with the bi pattern and stating degree with a complement after the verb.
Using the ba construction to move the object in front of the verb when you are saying what was done to it.
Reading short connected passages with no pinyin underneath them.
Separating the completed action particle from guo for past experience and zhe for a state that continues.
Making telephone calls, appointments and simple travel arrangements in Mandarin.
Writing a paragraph by hand and checking your own stroke order, spacing and character proportion.
Working through the listening, reading and writing sections of an HSK 3 paper against the clock.

curriculum.title: Level 4 - Independent Mandarin
topics: Growing into the vocabulary an HSK 4 paper assumes, grouped by subject rather than memorised as loose lists.
Reporting what happened to someone with the bei passive, which Chinese uses far more sparingly than English does.
Linking clauses with the paired connectors that carry although, not only and even if.
Holding an opinion, agreeing and disagreeing politely across a sustained discussion.
Reading news items and short essays and summarising them in Mandarin rather than in English.
Recognising common four-character chengyu and using a few of them where they genuinely fit.
Writing a structured composition whose paragraphs follow a single line of thought.

curriculum.title: Level 5 - Fluent and Cultural Mandarin
topics: Following films, interviews and broadcasts at full speed without subtitles, across the northern er ending and the softer southern accents.
Meeting the formal and classically flavoured constructions that appear in writing but almost never in speech.
Discussing business, technology and current affairs with the vocabulary each subject demands.
Reading how indirectness, politeness and face steer a Chinese conversation and adjusting what you say accordingly.
Reading longer authentic texts and inferring unfamiliar characters from context instead of stopping to look each one up.
Writing analytical pieces of several hundred characters that hold to one clear argument.
Telling mainland, Taiwanese and Singaporean usage apart in vocabulary, accent and written form.

curriculum.title: Level 6 - Certification and Professional Mandarin
topics: Sitting complete timed HSK mocks and learning how the paper is scored section by section out of three hundred marks.
Recording answers for the HSKK speaking test, which is spoken into a microphone with no examiner in the room.
Relaying figures, dates, quantities and delivery terms accurately in both directions during a simulated supplier call.
Writing professional email, meeting notes and a Chinese-style self-introduction.
Knowing that the HSK syllabus was rebuilt in 2021 into a nine-band scheme and which band matches the level you have reached.
Negotiating price, lead time and payment terms in the vocabulary Indian importers and exporters actually use.
Collecting recordings and written work into a portfolio, alongside an HSK score report that stays valid for two years.
Setting a review routine so that hard-won character recognition does not fade once the examination is over.

short_description: Live one-to-one Mandarin coaching, from tones to HSK certification.

name: Russian
subtitle: Live one-to-one Russian coaching, from the Cyrillic alphabet to TORFL certification.

curriculum.title: Level 1 - The Cyrillic Alphabet and First Russian
topics: Reading and handwriting all thirty-three Cyrillic letters from scratch, including the ones that look Latin and sound nothing like it.
Placing the stress correctly in every new word, since an unstressed o slides towards a and ordinary print never marks the stress for you.
Greeting people, choosing between the familiar and the polite you, and addressing an adult by first name and patronymic.
Learning each noun with its ending so that its gender is clear before you try to change it.
Conjugating present-tense verbs in the first and second patterns and leaving out the verb to be, which Russian simply does not use in the present.
Saying where something is or where you study with the prepositional case after v and na.
Counting, telling the time and quoting prices in roubles beside familiar rupee figures.

curriculum.title: Level 2 - The Case System Begins
topics: Using the accusative for direct objects and noticing that animate masculine nouns borrow the genitive form instead.
Handling the genitive for possession, absence and quantity, with the singular after two, three and four and the plural from five upwards.
Forming the past tense, which agrees with gender and number and ignores person altogether.
Talking about family, food, shopping and daily routine in guided conversation.
Using the dative for indirect objects, for stating age and for the liking construction where the person is not the subject.
Making adjectives agree with their noun in gender, number and case all at the same time.
Writing short messages and filling in simple forms in Russian.

curriculum.title: Level 3 - Aspect, Motion and Full Declension
topics: Choosing between imperfective and perfective verbs according to whether the action is presented as completed.
Separating the verbs of motion that describe one trip in one direction from those that describe repeated or return journeys.
Completing the case system with the instrumental, used for the tool, the means and after prepositions such as s.
Adding prefixes to motion verbs to say entering, leaving, crossing and approaching.
Declining pronouns and numerals accurately inside connected speech rather than in isolation.
Managing travel, health and accommodation situations in extended role-play.
Reading adapted texts aloud with correct stress and the rising contour that turns a statement into a question without any extra word.
Meeting the five subtests of the elementary TORFL examination, which assesses grammar and vocabulary separately from the four skills.

curriculum.title: Level 4 - Independent Russian
topics: Using aspect correctly in the future, in the imperative and after modal expressions such as nado and nelzya.
Building complex sentences with relative clauses, purpose clauses and conditional constructions.
Reporting what somebody else said and expressing opinion, doubt and agreement.
Reading news articles and short stories and summarising them in your own Russian.
Recognising participles and verbal adverbs, which fill written Russian and almost never surface in conversation.
Hearing how fast speech contracts, so that a long greeting or the word for now comes out far shorter than it looks on the page.
Discussing work, study and culture for several minutes without switching back into English.
Writing a structured letter or essay of around two hundred words.

curriculum.title: Level 5 - Mastery, Certification and Working Russian
topics: Sitting full timed TORFL mocks across all five subtests and clearing roughly two thirds of the marks in each, which is what the examination demands.
Watching films and current affairs programmes without subtitles and catching the irony Russian carries in word order and intonation rather than in vocabulary.
Presenting an argument and defending it in an unscripted exchange with your tutor.
Writing professional correspondence, a Russian rezyume and a formal application.
Handling the technical and commercial vocabulary that engineering, medicine and trade with Russia actually use.
Knowing that Russian universities generally ask for the first certificate level before admitting a degree student.
Reading a literary extract and discussing its register and imagery, including how Russian verse leans on stress rather than on syllable count.
Assembling recordings and written work into a portfolio that shows an employer or a university where your Russian now stands.

short_description: Live one-to-one Russian coaching, from the Cyrillic alphabet to TORFL certification.

name: Sanskrit
subtitle: Live Sanskrit coaching, from the varnamala to shloka and CBSE papers.

curriculum.title: Varnamala and First Words
topics: Reciting the varnamala in its traditional order and hearing how the sounds are grouped by the place they are made in the mouth.
Writing every Devanagari vowel and consonant with the correct stroke order and headline.
Producing the five vargas in turn from the throat to the lips and feeling where each sound is formed.
Reading simple Sanskrit words built from single consonants and their matra signs.
Greeting a teacher and classmates and introducing yourself using नमस्ते and your नाम.
Naming numbers, days of the week, family members and everyday objects in Sanskrit.
Chanting a short two-line prayer verse in unison, matching the group's rhythm and pace.

curriculum.title: Nouns, Verbs and Simple Sentences
topics: Declining the common a-ending masculine noun through all seven vibhaktis and the sambodhana vocative in the singular.
Recognising the three numbers of Sanskrit, singular, dual and plural, and why the dual matters.
Conjugating a bhvadi-gana dhatu in the present lat lakara across all nine of its forms.
Building simple sentences in which subject and verb agree in both person and number.
Using the three genders correctly with the pronouns सः, सा and तत्.
Reading and translating short conversational passages set in a school or a home.
Learning a handful of subhashita verses and explaining the moral of each in your own words.

curriculum.title: Vibhakti, Dhatu and Sandhi
topics: Working through the shabda roopa of nouns ending in a, i, u and consonants across all three numbers.
Learning the karaka relations that decide which vibhakti a word takes inside a sentence.
Conjugating dhatus in the past, future and imperative lakaras and knowing when each is used.
Applying the main swara sandhi rules such as dirgha, guna and vriddhi to join words.
Splitting a sandhi back into its component parts, which is how examination questions usually ask it.
Distinguishing parasmaipada from atmanepada verbs and choosing the correct set of endings.
Translating short Sanskrit paragraphs into English and back again with accurate case endings.

curriculum.title: Sandhi, Samas and Pratyaya in Depth
topics: Completing the vyanjana and visarga sandhi rules and applying them in continuous writing.
Identifying the four main types of samas and expanding each compound into its vigraha form.
Forming words with krit pratyayas such as क्त्वा, ल्यप् and तुमुन्, which build fresh words directly from a dhatu.
Forming words with taddhita pratyayas such as मतुप् and त्व, which build fresh words from an existing noun.
Using avyaya indeclinables and the numerals accurately in sentences you compose yourself.
Reading unseen prose passages and answering comprehension questions in Sanskrit.
Writing a short paragraph, letter or dialogue in simple but grammatically correct Sanskrit.
Reciting longer shlokas with attention to pauses, vowel length and the joins between words.

curriculum.title: Texts, Recitation and CBSE Paper Practice
topics: Reading graded extracts of classical narrative prose and paraphrasing them back in Sanskrit.
Chanting selected classical verses with correct vowel length, pause and breath control, a practice quite distinct from Vedic svara chanting.
Scanning simple metres such as anushtubh and hearing why a given line scans as it does.
Drilling the grammar sections that carry the highest weight in the CBSE Sanskrit paper.
Answering translation, anvaya and question-answer items under timed examination conditions.
Writing chitra-varnanam picture descriptions and short essays to the prescribed word counts.
Reviewing complete practice papers against a marking scheme and correcting recurring errors.

curriculum.title: Classical Reading and Independent Study
topics: Reading unedited verses from the epics and the Gita with a dictionary and a grammar reference to hand.
Producing your own anvaya word order and a word-by-word gloss for an unfamiliar verse.
Discussing the ideas contained in a passage with your tutor in spoken Sanskrit.
Tracing a single dhatu through its derived nouns and adjectives to see how Sanskrit builds vocabulary.
Comparing two published translations of the same verse and judging which keeps more of the original.
Preparing and performing a shloka recitation from memory for a family or school audience.
Compiling a personal notebook of verses, translations and grammar notes as a lasting reference.

short_description: Live Sanskrit coaching, from the varnamala to shloka and CBSE papers.

name: Hindi
subtitle: Live one-to-one Hindi, from the Devanagari alphabet to fluent speech.

curriculum.title: Devanagari Foundations
topics: Recognising and writing every Devanagari vowel with the correct stroke order and letter proportions, adding the shirorekha headline last.
Sounding out the consonant rows and hearing the difference between unaspirated and aspirated pairs such as क and ख.
Attaching matra signs to a single consonant so that it can be read as का, कि, की and कु.
Reading two- and three-letter words aloud from flashcards without leaning on Roman transliteration.
Greeting family members, introducing yourself and stating your age in short complete sentences.
Naming everyday household objects, colours and the numbers up to twenty in Hindi.
Copying short words neatly into a four-line notebook so that every letter hangs correctly from the shirorekha.

curriculum.title: Words, Sentences and Everyday Speech
topics: Forming conjunct consonants such as क्ष, त्र and ज्ञ and spotting them inside familiar words.
Using the anusvara and chandrabindu correctly so that nasal sounds are written the way they are spoken.
Building simple sentences in the subject-object-verb order that Hindi follows.
Matching verbs to masculine and feminine nouns so that gender agreement sounds natural.
Asking and answering questions about family, the school day and favourite food in short conversations.
Reading a six-line illustrated story aloud and retelling it in your own words.
Writing a five-sentence paragraph about yourself with correct word spacing and punctuation.

curriculum.title: The Grammar That Holds Hindi Together
topics: Working through the present, past and future tenses and choosing the right auxiliary verb for each.
Applying the karak case relations and the postpositions को, से, में and पर that signal them.
Handling the ergative ने construction in the past tense, where the verb agrees with the object rather than the subject.
Expanding vocabulary with prefixes and suffixes to build whole word families from one root.
Reading a page of graded prose and answering comprehension questions in full Hindi sentences.
Writing a short letter to a relative using the polite आप register and standard salutations.
Practising the polite, familiar and intimate forms of address and knowing when each is appropriate.

curriculum.title: Reading, Writing and Register
topics: Distinguishing tatsam words inherited from Sanskrit from tadbhav forms, deshaj regional words and videshaj loanwords taken from Persian, Arabic and English.
Using idioms and proverbs naturally in speech and explaining their figurative meaning.
Forming compound words through samas and breaking each one back into its vigrah.
Writing a structured essay of about two hundred words with an introduction, body and conclusion.
Composing formal and informal letters, applications and notices in the layouts board papers expect.
Summarising a newspaper article in Hindi and identifying the writer's main argument.
Reciting a short poem with attention to rhythm, pause and clear articulation.

curriculum.title: Literature and Board Preparation
topics: Reading extracts of modern Hindi prose and discussing character, setting and the writer's intent.
Analysing poetry for figures of speech such as anupras, upma and rupak, quoting evidence from the text.
Answering unseen passage questions under timed conditions in the way board papers are set.
Drilling the grammar sections that carry the heaviest marks, including sandhi, samas and vachya.
Writing descriptive, narrative and argumentative pieces to the word counts examiners specify.
Attempting full past-paper style question sets and reviewing them against a marking scheme.
Building a personal vocabulary log of literary words met in class and reusing them in your writing.

curriculum.title: Fluency, Debate and Independent Writing
topics: Holding a fifteen-minute discussion in Hindi on a current affairs topic without slipping into English.
Delivering a prepared speech with appropriate pace, projection and eye contact.
Debating both sides of a motion and rebutting an opponent's point in fluent Hindi.
Reading an unabridged short story and writing a critical review of it.
Translating a passage between English and Hindi while keeping the tone of the original.
Writing a feature article or blog post of five hundred words aimed at a real reader.
Assembling a portfolio of your best written work and recorded speech from the whole programme.

short_description: Live one-to-one Hindi, from the Devanagari alphabet to fluent speech.

name: Tamil
subtitle: Live Tamil lessons covering script, spoken Tamil and literary Tamil.

curriculum.title: Uyir, Mei and the First Letters
topics: Reciting and writing the twelve uyir vowels, watching how each short and long pair differs by a single added stroke.
Sounding out the eighteen mei consonants and using the pulli dot that marks a consonant carrying no vowel.
Sorting letters by ear into the three families Tamil grammar names, the hard vallinam, the soft mellinam and the medium idaiyinam.
Reading short two-syllable words aloud from picture cards without leaning on Roman transliteration.
Greeting elders with a respectful vanakkam and introducing yourself with your name and your town.
Naming colours, the numbers up to twenty, fruits and family relations in Tamil.
Writing your own name in Tamil script and keeping the letters evenly sized between ruled lines.

curriculum.title: The Uyirmei Grid and Everyday Words
topics: Building the full uyirmei grid of two hundred and sixteen compound letters, working through one consonant row at a time.
Explaining how the Tamil alphabet reaches its total of two hundred and forty-seven letters once every group is counted.
Recognising the aytham letter and the grantha letters Tamil keeps for words taken from Sanskrit and English.
Noticing how a hard vallinam letter softens between vowels, so the same letter is voiced differently depending on where it sits.
Building simple sentences in the subject-object-verb order that Tamil follows.
Talking about your day, your meals and your school routine in short spoken exchanges.
Reading a page of a graded storybook aloud with growing speed and accuracy.
Writing five sentences about your family with correct spacing and punctuation.

curriculum.title: Spoken Tamil Beside Written Tamil
topics: Learning how the spoken koduntamil heard at home differs from the centamil used in books, and why Tamil keeps both alive side by side.
Switching deliberately between the casual register used with friends and the formal register expected in class and on stage.
Using the singular, plural and honorific forms of address correctly with elders, teachers and younger children.
Attaching the vetrumai case suffixes to nouns so that a sentence shows plainly who is doing what to whom.
Conjugating verbs across the three tenses using the kaala idainilai tense markers that sit inside the verb itself.
Holding a five-minute conversation on a familiar topic without switching into English.
Reading a short news item written in formal Tamil and explaining it back in everyday spoken Tamil.

curriculum.title: Punarchi, Word Classes and Composition
topics: Applying the punarchi rules that decide how two Tamil words change shape at the point where they join.
Sorting words into the four classes Tamil grammar recognises, the peyarchol, vinaichol, idaichol and urichol.
Understanding how Tamil grammar is traditionally divided into eluttu and sol, and placing the rules you are learning within that scheme.
Using Tamil idioms and proverbs in speech and explaining the picture each one paints.
Answering comprehension questions on an unseen passage in complete Tamil sentences.
Writing a letter, an invitation and a notice in the formats Tamil school papers ask for.
Composing a descriptive essay of about a hundred and fifty words worked out from a written plan.

curriculum.title: Classical and Modern Tamil Literature
topics: Reading couplets from the Tirukkural, unpacking each one word by word before discussing the conduct it recommends.
Meeting the Sangam anthologies and the way they divide poems into the akam of inner life and the puram of public life.
Hearing the sound patterns Tamil verse is built on, including monai alliteration and the edhukai rhyme that falls on the second syllable.
Studying modern Tamil prose and discussing theme, character and the writer's viewpoint.
Drilling the grammar and vocabulary sections that carry the most marks in Tamil board papers.
Writing narrative, descriptive and argumentative answers to the word counts examiners prescribe.
Working through timed past-paper style question sets and reviewing them against a marking scheme.
Keeping a journal of literary words met in class and putting them to use in your own writing.

curriculum.title: Oratory, Translation and Portfolio
topics: Speaking for ten minutes on a prepared topic in clear centamil before an audience.
Debating a motion in Tamil and answering counter-arguments on the spot.
Reading an unabridged Tamil short story or novella and writing a critical review of it.
Translating between English and Tamil while preserving the idiom and tone of the original.
Performing a passage of verse from memory with the pauses and stress the metre asks for.
Writing a feature article of five hundred words aimed at a real Tamil-reading audience.
Assembling a portfolio of recorded recitations and written pieces from across the programme.

short_description: Live Tamil lessons covering script, spoken Tamil and literary Tamil.

name: Telugu
subtitle: Live Telugu lessons from the varnamala to fluent reading and speech.

curriculum.title: Achulu, Hallulu and First Words
topics: Reciting the achulu vowels in order and writing each one with the rounded strokes Telugu letters are built from.
Sounding out the hallulu consonants varga by varga and hearing where in the mouth each group is made.
Writing the talakattu head-stroke that sits on top of most Telugu letters so that it stays the same size every time.
Reading simple two-syllable words aloud from flashcards without any Roman transliteration.
Greeting elders respectfully and introducing yourself with your name and your family.
Naming the numbers up to twenty, colours, animals and household objects in Telugu.
Writing your own name and your family's names in Telugu script inside a ruled notebook.

curriculum.title: Gunintalu and First Sentences
topics: Adding the gunintalu vowel signs to a consonant so that a single letter can be read in every one of its vowel forms.
Reciting the complete gunintam of any consonant your tutor names, from memory and in the correct order.
Using the sunna nasal mark and the visarga correctly so that words are spelled the way they are said.
Reading three- and four-syllable words and short captioned sentences with confidence.
Building simple sentences in the subject-object-verb order that Telugu follows.
Talking about your day, your school and your favourite food in short spoken exchanges.
Reading a graded picture story aloud and retelling it in your own words.
Writing five neat sentences about your family with correct spacing between words.

curriculum.title: Vattulu, Verbs and Everyday Fluency
topics: Writing the vattulu subscript consonants and reading the ottakshara clusters they create inside words.
Pronouncing doubled consonants and longer clusters smoothly without breaking the flow of a sentence.
Attaching vibhakti case suffixes to nouns to show each word's role within the sentence.
Conjugating verbs in past, present and future so that they agree with the subject in person and number.
Handling the mahat and amahat distinction correctly, since Telugu treats human and non-human subjects differently.
Choosing between the respectful and the familiar forms of address depending on who you are speaking to.
Holding a five-minute conversation on a familiar topic entirely in Telugu.
Reading a short news item aloud and explaining what it says in your own words.

curriculum.title: Sandhi, Samasa and Composition
topics: Applying the native Telugu sandhis such as utva, itva and atva that join words at their boundaries.
Applying the Sanskrit-derived sandhis such as savarnadeergha and guna that Telugu uses alongside its own.
Telling tatsama words taken from Sanskrit apart from native tadbhava forms and desya vocabulary.
Forming compounds through samasa and breaking each one back into its vigraha vakyam.
Using Telugu idioms and proverbs in speech and explaining the image behind each of them.
Answering comprehension questions on an unseen passage in complete Telugu sentences.
Writing letters, applications and notices in the layouts school papers require.
Composing a descriptive essay of about a hundred and fifty words worked out from a plan.

curriculum.title: Padyam, Prose and Examination Preparation
topics: Reading classical padyam verse and working out its sense line by line through a pratipadartham word gloss.
Scanning a verse into its ganas and locating the yati and the prasa that fix where its sounds must echo.
Recognising the common metres by ear, including the compact kanda padyam and the long utpalamala and champakamala lines.
Reading sataka verse and discussing the moral each stanza is built around.
Studying modern Telugu prose extracts and discussing theme, character and the writer's purpose.
Drilling the grammar sections that carry the heaviest marks in state board Telugu papers.
Writing narrative, descriptive and argumentative answers to the prescribed word counts.
Attempting timed past-paper style question sets and reviewing them against a marking scheme.

curriculum.title: Fluency, Public Speaking and Portfolio
topics: Speaking for ten minutes on a prepared topic in clear formal Telugu.
Debating a motion in Telugu and answering counter-arguments without preparation.
Reading a full Telugu short story or novella and writing a critical review of it.
Translating between English and Telugu while keeping the tone of the original intact.
Reciting a classical padyam from memory with the pauses and vowel lengths its metre requires.
Writing a feature article of five hundred words for a real Telugu-reading audience.
Keeping a vocabulary journal of literary words and reusing them in your own writing.
Assembling a portfolio of recorded recitations and written pieces from the whole programme.

short_description: Live Telugu lessons from the varnamala to fluent reading and speech.

name: Kannada
subtitle: Live Kannada tuition, from the alphabet to fluent reading and writing.

curriculum.title: Swaragalu, Vyanjanagalu and First Words
topics: Reciting the swaragalu vowels in order and writing each one with the rounded Kannada stroke shapes.
Sounding out the vyanjanagalu consonants varga by varga and hearing how each group is articulated.
Learning the two yogavahagalu, the anusvara and the visarga, and where each attaches to a letter.
Reading simple two-syllable words aloud from picture cards without transliteration.
Greeting elders respectfully and introducing yourself in complete Kannada sentences.
Naming the numbers up to twenty, colours, fruits and family relations in Kannada.
Writing your own name and your family's names in Kannada script between ruled lines.

curriculum.title: Kagunita and First Sentences
topics: Adding kagunita vowel signs to a consonant so that one letter can be read in every one of its vowel forms.
Reciting the full kagunita of any consonant your tutor calls out, without looking at the chart.
Reading three- and four-syllable words and short captioned sentences fluently.
Building simple sentences in the subject-object-verb order that Kannada uses.
Talking about your day, your school and your meals in short spoken exchanges.
Reading a graded picture story aloud and retelling it in your own words.
Writing five neat sentences about your family with correct spacing and punctuation.

curriculum.title: Ottakshara, Vibhakti and Everyday Fluency
topics: Writing ottakshara subscript consonants and reading the clusters they form inside longer words.
Pronouncing conjunct clusters smoothly so that they never break the flow of a spoken sentence.
Attaching the vibhakti pratyayas to nouns to show each word's role inside the sentence.
Conjugating verbs across past, present and future so that they agree with the subject in person, gender and number.
Choosing between honorific and familiar address depending on who you are speaking to.
